ICML Sponsor Hotel & Function Space Requests – Required Process All guest room requests, including individual reservations and room blocks, must be submitted through the official ICML Housing Team. Availability is managed on a first-come, first-served basis, and this process is required to protect conference commitments and contracted agreements. All meeting and function space requests must be reviewed and approved by the ICML team before any arrangements can be made to ensure there are no conflicts with the official conference program. Please do not contact hotels directly. Hotels will refer all ICML-related requests back to the conference team, which will only delay the process. If your request does not conflict with the official program, we will work to assist you as quickly as possible. Following the official process is the fastest and most effective path forward. About the Conference The International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) is the premier gathering of professionals dedicated to the advancement of the branch of artificial intelligence known as machine learning. ICML is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of machine learning used in closely related areas like artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, and robotics. ICML is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICML span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs.

items.content: Submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing The number of submissions to ICML keeps growing faster than the number of qualified reviewers. To keep the review process fair and informative for all authors, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens its reciprocal reviewing requirement. These rules are similar to those adopted by ICLR 2027. Submission quotas No author may appear as a co-author on more than 20 submissions. Each author may appear as a co-author on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer (see below). In plain terms: if neither you nor any of your co-authors has published at one of the venues listed below, you may submit at most one paper to ICML 2027. We welcome submissions from researchers who are new to the field, and these submissions are reviewed like all others. Quotas are checked when abstracts are registered. Authors who exceed a quota will be notified and can fix the problem before the full paper deadline (January 22, 2027). If a quota is still exceeded at the full paper deadline, the program chairs will desk reject excess submissions at random until every author is within the quotas. Who is an eligible reciprocal reviewer An author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer if they have at least one paper accepted at one of the following venues by the abstract registration deadline (January 14, 2027): ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, UAI, AISTATS, JMLR, TMLR (including Datasets and Benchmarks tracks), ACL, EMNLP, EACL, NAACL, IJCNLP-AACL, Computational Linguistics, TACL (including Findings), COLM CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, TPAMI, AAAI, IJCAI, JAIR, 3DV ICRA, IROS, RSS, CoRL KDD COLT Other publications associated with these venues do not count. This includes workshop papers, position papers, short papers, system demonstrations, industry papers and blog posts. Eligibility is determined from OpenReview profiles, so all authors must keep their profiles complete and up to date, including their publications or DBLP link. Incorrect profile information may lead to desk rejection. Reciprocal reviewing requirement Per-submission requirement: each submission must designate one of its authors as its reciprocal reviewer when the abstract is registered. The designated author must: be an eligible reciprocal reviewer; register as a reviewer for ICML 2027; complete their assigned reviews during the reviewing period (February 24–March 16, 2027). An author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Submissions in which no author is eligible are exempt from this requirement, but they count toward the one-submission quota above. Per-author requirement: authors with 3 or more submissions must serve on the program committee of ICML 2027, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Authors who serve as area chairs, senior area chairs or members of the organizing committee meet this requirement through that role. Responsibilities and enforcement Reciprocal reviewers have the same obligations as all other reviewers. They must follow the reviewing guidelines and the LLM policy, submit their reviews on time, and take part in the discussion with authors and area chairs. The program chairs may desk reject the submissions for which an author is the designated reciprocal reviewer if that author: does not submit their reviews; submits reviews of very low quality; violates the LLM policy. Submissions that do not designate an eligible reciprocal reviewer when one is available among their authors may also be desk rejected.
items.raw_text: Submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing The number of submissions to ICML keeps growing faster than the number of qualified reviewers. To keep the review process fair and informative for all authors, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens its reciprocal reviewing requirement. These rules are similar to those adopted by ICLR 2027. Submission quotas No author may appear as a co-author on more than 20 submissions. Each author may appear as a co-author on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer (see below). In plain terms: if neither you nor any of your co-authors has published at one of the venues listed below, you may submit at most one paper to ICML 2027. We welcome submissions from researchers who are new to the field, and these submissions are reviewed like all others. Quotas are checked when abstracts are registered. Authors who exceed a quota will be notified and can fix the problem before the full paper deadline (January 22, 2027). If a quota is still exceeded at the full paper deadline, the program chairs will desk reject excess submissions at random until every author is within the quotas. Who is an eligible reciprocal reviewer An author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer if they have at least one paper accepted at one of the following venues by the abstract registration deadline (January 14, 2027): ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, UAI, AISTATS, JMLR, TMLR (including Datasets and Benchmarks tracks), ACL, EMNLP, EACL, NAACL, IJCNLP-AACL, Computational Linguistics, TACL (including Findings), COLM CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, TPAMI, AAAI, IJCAI, JAIR, 3DV ICRA, IROS, RSS, CoRL KDD COLT Other publications associated with these venues do not count. This includes workshop papers, position papers, short papers, system demonstrations, industry papers and blog posts. Eligibility is determined from OpenReview profiles, so all authors must keep their profiles complete and up to date, including their publications or DBLP link. Incorrect profile information may lead to desk rejection. Reciprocal reviewing requirement Per-submission requirement: each submission must designate one of its authors as its reciprocal reviewer when the abstract is registered. The designated author must: be an eligible reciprocal reviewer; register as a reviewer for ICML 2027; complete their assigned reviews during the reviewing period (February 24–March 16, 2027). An author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Submissions in which no author is eligible are exempt from this requirement, but they count toward the one-submission quota above. Per-author requirement: authors with 3 or more submissions must serve on the program committee of ICML 2027, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Authors who serve as area chairs, senior area chairs or members of the organizing committee meet this requirement through that role. Responsibilities and enforcement Reciprocal reviewers have the same obligations as all other reviewers. They must follow the reviewing guidelines and the LLM policy, submit their reviews on time, and take part in the discussion with authors and area chairs. The program chairs may desk reject the submissions for which an author is the designated reciprocal reviewer if that author: does not submit their reviews; submits reviews of very low quality; violates the LLM policy. Submissions that do not designate an eligible reciprocal reviewer when one is available among their authors may also be desk rejected.

ICLR is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of deep learning used in the fields of artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, text understanding, gaming, and robotics. ICLR is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICLR span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs. The rapidly developing field of deep learning is concerned with questions surrounding how we can best learn meaningful and useful representations of data. ICLR takes a broad view of the field and includes topics such as feature learning, metric learning, compositional modeling, structured prediction, reinforcement learning, and issues regarding large-scale learning and non-convex optimization. A non-exhaustive list of relevant topics explored at the conference include: Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, and Supervised Representation Learning Representation Learning for Planning and Reinforcement Learning Metric Learning and Kernel Learning Sparse Coding and Dimensionality Expansion Hierarchical Models Optimization for Representation Learning Learning Representations of Outputs or States Implementation Issues, Parallelization, Software Platforms, Hardware Applications in Vision, Audio, Speech, Natural Language Processing, Robotics, Neuroscience, or Any Other Field

items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. ACADEMIC CONFERENCE Microsoft at SOSP 2026 Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software. Learn more Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . items.raw_text: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. ACADEMIC CONFERENCE Microsoft at SOSP 2026 Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software. Learn more Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. items.content: Alex Shtoff TorchCruves: Differentiable Parametric Curves Alex Shtoff alex.shtf@gmail.com Abstract We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov–Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves . † † heading: 23 2022 1- 1/21; Revised 5/22 9/22 21-0000 † † shortheadings: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves / TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves † † firstpage: 1 keywords spline, kolmogorov-arnold-network, kan, machine-learning 1 Introduction Figure 1: The basic operation behind TorchCurves. Input: a mini-batch of numerical features of size. Output: a mini-batch of points on multi-dimensional curves. The use of parametric curves spans a wide variety of scientific and engineing disciplines, both in machine learning and outside of it. Examples include spline regression, continuous features embeddings ( Shtoff et al., 2024 ) , Kolmogorov-Anrnold networks ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , computer aided design ( Bézier, 1968 ) and others. Yet, there seems to be no software library providing a common, composable interface for curves as learnable primitives, but rather every re-implements its own high-level object directly. TorchCurves puts the learnable parametric curve as a primitive in its own right, and facilitates its use in a variety of model achitectures. Its genericity allows PyTorch ( Ansel et al., 2024 ) users to build models that include learnable parametric curves as a component. The essence of TorchCurves is one operation - transforming a mini-batch of input features to a mini-batch of points on curves in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , as depicted in Figure 1 . At this stage we support B-Spline and Legendre polynomials. Our implementation is vectorized and there are no loops on the feature, batch and curve dimensions. But we do not have custom kernels for specialized hardware - we chose to implement everything in pure PyTorch for readability and maintainability reasons. This basic operation is differentiable in both its parameters, the input features and the curve parameters, allowing both learning a curve and back-propagating to previous network layers. The next sections are structures as follows: in Section 3 we present the main components of the library and present examples of applications: continuous feature embeddings, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, and functional regression. In Section 4 we discuss some implementation and testing details. 2 Related work Polynomial and spline representations are well established in numerical software. NumPy ( Harris et al., 2020 ) and SciPy ( Virtanen et al., 2020 ) provide routines for representing, evaluating, and differentiating such functions. Differentiable spline packages also exist within the PyTorch ecosystem: torchcubicspline ( Kidger, n.d. ) constructs natural cubic interpolants from observations, while torch-bspline ( Melchers and Cochran, 2025 ) provides differentiable B-spline evaluation. In machine learning, mappings from scalar values to learned vectors appear in numerical feature embeddings ( Gorishniy et al., 2022 ; Shtoff et al., 2024 ) . Learnable univariate functions also constitute the edges of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , with specialized implementations such as EfficientKAN ( Cao, 2024 ) . These applications illustrate several roles that parametric curves can play within a larger model. TorchCurves takes the curve itself as the reusable abstraction: a parameterized mapping from a scalar input to a vector output, differentiable with respect to both its input and its coefficients. It provides a common interface for B-spline and Legendre polynomial representations, whose coefficients can be learned directly or supplied by another model. Its contribution is to make these curves convenient to compose with other learning components, without requiring an interpolation problem or prescribing a particular network architecture. 3 API and applications We first present the basic API, and then show use-case examples where it can serve. 3.1 The API The library provides two basic components, BSplineCurve and LegendreCurves , which are one-dimensional curves embedded in a high-dimensional space. Each curve is represented as 𝒄 ⁡ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 n 𝒗 i ​ B i ​ ( x ) , {\bm{c}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\bm{v}}_{i}B_{i}(x), where B i B_{i} are the appropriate basis functions, B-Spline or Legendre, and 𝒗 1 , … , 𝒗 n {\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{n} are its (possibly) learned coefficients. Each component can evaluate a bulk of curves 𝒄 1 , … , 𝒄 m {\bm{c}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{c}}_{m} simultaneously, as shown in Figure 1 . Below is an example: ⬇ import torch import torchcurves as tc u = torch . rand (4, 3) # 4 samples with 3 features. curve = tc . BSplineCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =2 # 3 curves in 2 dimensions ) y = curve ( u ) # (4 samples, 3 curves, 2 dimensions) print ( u . shape , ”->” , y . shape ) # torch.Size([4, 3]) -> torch.Size([4, 5, 2]) Of course, mathemaically inclined readers will say this example is incomplete. And justifiably so - both B-Spline and Legendre polynomial bases require configuration, such as the polynomial degree, the number of knots in case of B-Splines, and others. Moreover, splines and polynomial approximations work in a compact interval , which is nowhere to be seen in the above example. Indeed, we provide the modules with defaults, but they are are fully configurable. Both B-Splines and Legendre polynomials are assumed to approximate inputs on the interval 𝒰 = [ − 1 , 1 ] \mathcal{U}=[-1,1] , and can be configured with a mapping for transforming their input to that interval. For example: ⬇ spl_curve = tc . BSplineCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =2, # dimensions input_map = ’real.arctan’ , # maps ‘x‘ to ‘2 arctan(x) pi‘ num_knots =20, # 20 uniformly-spaced knots, with not-a-knot endpoints degree =5 # polynomial splines of degree 5 ) lgd_curve = tc . LegendreCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =5 # dimensions input_map = ’arctan’ , # same as above degree =50 # degree-50 Legendre polynomials ) Mapping functions include the above-mentioned arctangent function, which is also the default, but also x → x / 1 + x 2 x\to x/\sqrt{1+x^{2}} called real.rational and is inspired by by its use in the differential equations literature on unbounded domains ( Guo and Wang, 2004 ; Boyd, 1987 ; Wang and Guo, 2004 ) , and a simple clamping to 𝒰 \mathcal{U} called real.clamp . The prefix real means these mappings are designed for arbitrary real numbers. The library also has nonneg.rational and nonneg.arctan for non-negative numbers. The users can also provide their own, in the form of a Python callable. Trainable modules are useful, but they do not cover all use-cases the library aims to support. Thus, the library provides three API levels which we shall explain below: (a) trainable modules, as we just seen; (b) basis modules, which cache tensors to avoid their recomputation but have no trainable parameters; (c) a fully functional API, akin to torch.nn.functional . The fully functional API, as its name suggests, consists of pure functions that have no state. Below is an example: ⬇ import torchcurves . functional as tcf bspl_func = tcf . bspline_curves ( inputs , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs , # (C, P, D) coefficients of C B-Spline functions having P coefficients in D dimensions knots , # B-Spline knots. unif. spaced in [-1, 1] with not-a-knot conditions, if unspecified. degree =5 # the piecewise-polynomial degree. 3 if unspecified. ) leg_func = tcf . legendre_curves ( inputs , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs , # (C, P, D) coefficients of C legendre polynomials having P coefficinets in D dimensions degree =50 # the polynomial degree. We always have P=degree-1. These are useful if the coefficients are not learned directly, but come as an output of another module. Note, that in case of B-Spline functions, the connection between the number of knots and the number of coefficients P must be 𝙿 = | 𝚔𝚗𝚘𝚝𝚜 | − 𝚍𝚎𝚐𝚛𝚎𝚎 + 1 \mathtt{P}=|\mathtt{knots}|-\mathtt{degree}+1 . If the knot vector is not specified, the number of uniformly-spaced knots is automatically determined from the degree and the number of coefficients P . Finally, in between learnable modules and fully functional API we have the basis modules. A basis module is similar to the functional API, but stores immutable buffers, such as the knot vector, for convenience. That way, if a model is moved from CPU to an accelerator, such as a GPU, the buffer automatically moves with it by PyTorch. Below is an example: ⬇ import torchcurves as tc # quadratic splines with 50 B-Spline functions and a rational mapping to [-1, 1] bspl_basis = tc . BSplineBasis ( degree =2, knot_config =50, input_map = ”real.rational” ) # evaluate a B-Spline function. Note - 50 coefficients for our 50 B-Spline functions. bspl_func = bspl_basis ( input , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs # (C, 50, D) - the coefficients of C B-Spline functions in D dimensions. ) 3.2 Applications One of the first applications that comes to mind is producing embeddings for continuous features, such as height, weight, BMI, the time since the last visit of the user on our website, and others. Imagine we have a model whose inputs are embedding vectors, such as a Factorization Machine, or a Transformer. For discrete, or categorical features - we can just map features to embeddings using a standard embedding table. But for a continuous value, we need a mapping of the value to a vector in the embedding space - and a curve is such a mapping. Here is an example that uses Legendre polynomial basis for such curves: ⬇ from torch import nn , cat import torchcurves as tc class Net ( nn . Module ): ”” ”Composes ␣ PyTorch ␣ ‘nn.Embedding‘ ␣ and ␣ Legendre ␣ curves ␣ with ␣ another ␣ model” ”” def __init__ ( self , n_discrete , n_continuous , degree , dim ): super (). __init__ () self . discrete = nn . Embedding ( n_discrete , dim ) self . cont = tc . LegendreCurve ( n_continuous , dim , degree ) self . inner_model = my_super_duper_transformer () def forward ( self , cat , cont ): # concatenate all embeddings into one tensor embeddings = cat (( self . discrete ( cat ), self . cont ( cont )), dim =-2) # invoke our desired model on the embeddings return self . inner_model ( embeddings ) Kolmogorov-Arnold networks are also an immediate application - each layer computes many univariate functions of the input, and sums-up their results. Recalling that the output of our curve layers has the shape (sample, curve, dimension) , a KAN layer just applies our curve layer, followed by a sum over the curve dimension. For convenience, we include the Sum module in the library as well. Here is an example: ⬇ from torch import nn import torchcurves as tc kan = nn . Sequential ([ # layer 1 tc . BSplineCurve ( input_dim , hidden_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), # layer 2 tc . BSplineCurve ( hidden_dim , hidden_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), # layer 3 tc . BSplineCurve ( hidden_dim , output_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), ]) A less trivial application is that of functional regression - a model whose output is itself a function. In theory, we can think of any model f ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) f({\bm{x}}) as ”functional regression” - just partition 𝒙 = ( 𝒙 1 , 𝒙 2 ) {\bm{x}}=({\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}) and define the model as the function f ⁡ ( 𝒙 1 , ⋅ ) f({\bm{x}}_{1},\cdot) . The point is not in the model’s architecture, but as the study of the model, including its performance, as such a function. Since the authors come from the online advertising field, one prominent example is fitting the probability of winning an ad auction given auction features and a non-negative bid. See Pan et al. (2020) ; Zhou et al. (2021) . Note that this is a CDF - it must be nondecreasing. A natural choice is using the property of B-Spline functions - if the coefficient vector is non-decreasing, so is the function. So below is such an example - we encode the auction into a non-decreasing vector of coefficients, which in turn serves as the coefficient vector of a B-Spline function of the bid. So below is a model for learning such a probability: ⬇ from torch import nn import torch . nn . functional as F import torchcurves as tc class AuctionWinModel ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self ): super (). __init__ () self . encoder = MySuperBestAuctionEncoder () self . spline = tc . BSplineBasis ( input_map = ”nonneg.arctan” ) def forward ( self , auction_features , bids ): # encode auction to a latent vector raw = self . encoder ( auction_features ) # convert the latent vector to non-decreasing coefficients: # use first component as is, add cumulative sum of softplus(rest) increments = F . softplus ( raw [:, 1:]) coefficients = raw [:, :1] + F . pad ( increments . cumsum (-1), (1, 0)) # non-decreasing spline function of bids to produce P(win) logits. return self . spline ( bids [ None ], coefficients […, None ]). flatten () 4 Algorithms Beyond being vectorized, the implementations we use should also be fairly efficient to be useful for machine learning research. Our efficiency goals are modest - we aim for the best we can achieve using pure PyTorch code, without custom kernels. Thus, we implement vectorized versions of well-known algorithms, both for B-Spline and Legendre polynomial evaluation. The main feature of the B-Spline basis is its sparsity - at any given point, only 𝚍𝚎𝚐𝚛𝚎𝚎 + 2 \mathtt{degree}+2 basis functions are non-zero. An efficient algorithm for exploiting the sparsity is the well-known Cox-deBoor method ( COX, 1972 ; De Boor, 1972 ) . The algorithm provides both an efficient sparsity-exploiting way to compute the value and the derivative. These, in turn, are used in a custom PyTorch autograd function to facilitate efficient back-propagation through the inputs and the coefficients. The implementation is done in a vectorized manner without iterating on any of the input dimension, but does require iterating on the degree. Thus, a spline of degree five does require six Python iterations to compute. For Legendre polynomials we have the well-known Clenshaw recursion ( Clenshaw, 1955 ) . Here, as well, we do not iterate on any input tensor dimensions, but we do iterate on the degree. Since typically good approximation is achieved with high-degree polynomials, higher than B-Splines, this may be less efficient in some situations. For example, a polynomial of degree 50 will require 51 Python for-loop iterations. In our implementation we do take special care to avoid memory allocation of tensors. We do not claim optimality, but merely a best-effort. Again, our efficiency claim is modest - to be fast enough to be useful. The library is thoroughly tested, and in particular, the results are compared to SciPy ( Virtanen et al., 2020 ) splines and NumPy ( Harris et al., 2020 ) Legendre polynomials. Derivatives are validated using internal gradient-checking mechanisms of PyTorch, that compare numerically approximated derivatives to those of back-propagation. Comparisons were done for both 32 and 64 bit floating point numbers. 5 Experiments Our objective here is giving the reader a qualitative understanding of what we mean by ”our efficiency claim is modest”. To that end, we perform two comparisons: (a) speed of inference-only computation of Legendre polynomials and Splines on CPU, compared to NumPy and SciPy; and (b) training speed of a KAN, compared to EfficientKAN ( Cao, 2024 ) , both on CPU and GPU, each implemented in its idiomatic form. Our aim is not to outperform specialized implementations, but to show that the flexibility of treating curves as general-purpose trainable primitives remains computationally practical, even when composing them into higher-level architectures such as KANs. All measurements were done on a Lenovo P14s Gen-7 laptop, with an Intel Core Ultra 7 356H CPU, and a NVIDIA RTX PRO 500 Blackwell GPU. The experiments were running on Ubuntu 26.04.01, with Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5.4, SciPy 1.18.1, and PyTorch 2.15 (CUDA 13.2). CPU affinity is limited to the first cores 1-4, which are the performance cores of that CPU, to both allow PyTorch exploit parallelism and obtain consistent speed measurements. We note that both NumPy and SciPy do not provide an autograd mechanism, thus they are by definition “inference-only” libraries. Therefore, our comparison in (a) are inference-only in nature - we perform no backpropagation, but only compute the value of the spline / Legendre polynomial functions using each library, and compare the number of milliseconds per call for various coefficient counts, curve dimensions, curve counts, and batch sizes. The results are in Figures 2 and 3 . We can see that torchcurves is slower for small number of curves or small batch sizes, and in the ballpark or faster for larger scales. It is our conjecture that at smaller scales Python overhead wins, whereas for larger scales vectorized PyTorch code lets it exploit multiple cores, while NumPy and SciPy remain serial. In all cases, we perform Figure 2: CPU evaluation of independent vector-valued B-Spline curves. Panel rows show curve count C; panel columns show output dimension D. Within each panel, rows show batch size B and columns show coefficients per scalar output K. Each cell is median TorchCurves time divided by median SciPy time. Values below 1 mean TorchCurves is faster. Medians use five timing measurements. Figure 3: CPU evaluation of independent vector-valued Legendre-polynomial curves. Panel rows show curve count C; panel columns show output dimension D. Within each panel, rows show batch size B and columns show coefficients per scalar output K. items.raw_text: Alex Shtoff TorchCruves: Differentiable Parametric Curves Alex Shtoff alex.shtf@gmail.com Abstract We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov–Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves . † † heading: 23 2022 1- 1/21; Revised 5/22 9/22 21-0000 † † shortheadings: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves / TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves † † firstpage: 1 keywords spline, kolmogorov-arnold-network, kan, machine-learning 1 Introduction Figure 1: The basic operation behind TorchCurves. Input: a mini-batch of numerical features of size. Output: a mini-batch of points on multi-dimensional curves. The use of parametric curves spans a wide variety of scientific and engineing disciplines, both in machine learning and outside of it. Examples include spline regression, continuous features embeddings ( Shtoff et al., 2024 ) , Kolmogorov-Anrnold networks ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , computer aided design ( Bézier, 1968 ) and others. Yet, there seems to be no software library providing a common, composable interface for curves as learnable primitives, but rather every re-implements its own high-level object directly. TorchCurves puts the learnable parametric curve as a primitive in its own right, and facilitates its use in a variety of model achitectures. Its genericity allows PyTorch ( Ansel et al., 2024 ) users to build models that include learnable parametric curves as a component. The essence of TorchCurves is one operation - transforming a mini-batch of input features to a mini-batch of points on curves in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , as depicted in Figure 1 . At this stage we support B-Spline and Legendre polynomials. Our implementation is vectorized and there are no loops on the feature, batch and curve dimensions. But we do not have custom kernels for specialized hardware - we chose to implement everything in pure PyTorch for readability and maintainability reasons. This basic operation is differentiable in both its parameters, the input features and the curve parameters, allowing both learning a curve and back-propagating to previous network layers. The next sections are structures as follows: in Section 3 we present the main components of the library and present examples of applications: continuous feature embeddings, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, and functional regression. In Section 4 we discuss some implementation and testing details. 2 Related work Polynomial and spline representations are well established in numerical software. NumPy ( Harris et al., 2020 ) and SciPy ( Virtanen et al., 2020 ) provide routines for representing, evaluating, and differentiating such functions. Differentiable spline packages also exist within the PyTorch ecosystem: torchcubicspline ( Kidger, n.d. ) constructs natural cubic interpolants from observations, while torch-bspline ( Melchers and Cochran, 2025 ) provides differentiable B-spline evaluation. In machine learning, mappings from scalar values to learned vectors appear in numerical feature embeddings ( Gorishniy et al., 2022 ; Shtoff et al., 2024 ) . Learnable univariate functions also constitute the edges of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , with specialized implementations such as EfficientKAN ( Cao, 2024 ) . These applications illustrate several roles that parametric curves can play within a larger model. TorchCurves takes the curve itself as the reusable abstraction: a parameterized mapping from a scalar input to a vector output, differentiable with respect to both its input and its coefficients. It provides a common interface for B-spline and Legendre polynomial representations, whose coefficients can be learned directly or supplied by another model. Its contribution is to make these curves convenient to compose with other learning components, without requiring an interpolation problem or prescribing a particular network architecture. 3 API and applications We first present the basic API, and then show use-case examples where it can serve. 3.1 The API The library provides two basic components, BSplineCurve and LegendreCurves , which are one-dimensional curves embedded in a high-dimensional space. Each curve is represented as 𝒄 ⁡ ( x ) = ∑ i = 1 n 𝒗 i ​ B i ​ ( x ) , {\bm{c}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\bm{v}}_{i}B_{i}(x), where B i B_{i} are the appropriate basis functions, B-Spline or Legendre, and 𝒗 1 , … , 𝒗 n {\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{n} are its (possibly) learned coefficients. Each component can evaluate a bulk of curves 𝒄 1 , … , 𝒄 m {\bm{c}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{c}}_{m} simultaneously, as shown in Figure 1 . Below is an example: ⬇ import torch import torchcurves as tc u = torch . rand (4, 3) # 4 samples with 3 features. curve = tc . BSplineCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =2 # 3 curves in 2 dimensions ) y = curve ( u ) # (4 samples, 3 curves, 2 dimensions) print ( u . shape , ”->” , y . shape ) # torch.Size([4, 3]) -> torch.Size([4, 5, 2]) Of course, mathemaically inclined readers will say this example is incomplete. And justifiably so - both B-Spline and Legendre polynomial bases require configuration, such as the polynomial degree, the number of knots in case of B-Splines, and others. Moreover, splines and polynomial approximations work in a compact interval , which is nowhere to be seen in the above example. Indeed, we provide the modules with defaults, but they are are fully configurable. Both B-Splines and Legendre polynomials are assumed to approximate inputs on the interval 𝒰 = [ − 1 , 1 ] \mathcal{U}=[-1,1] , and can be configured with a mapping for transforming their input to that interval. For example: ⬇ spl_curve = tc . BSplineCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =2, # dimensions input_map = ’real.arctan’ , # maps ‘x‘ to ‘2 arctan(x) pi‘ num_knots =20, # 20 uniformly-spaced knots, with not-a-knot endpoints degree =5 # polynomial splines of degree 5 ) lgd_curve = tc . LegendreCurve ( num_curves =3, dim =5 # dimensions input_map = ’arctan’ , # same as above degree =50 # degree-50 Legendre polynomials ) Mapping functions include the above-mentioned arctangent function, which is also the default, but also x → x / 1 + x 2 x\to x/\sqrt{1+x^{2}} called real.rational and is inspired by by its use in the differential equations literature on unbounded domains ( Guo and Wang, 2004 ; Boyd, 1987 ; Wang and Guo, 2004 ) , and a simple clamping to 𝒰 \mathcal{U} called real.clamp . The prefix real means these mappings are designed for arbitrary real numbers. The library also has nonneg.rational and nonneg.arctan for non-negative numbers. The users can also provide their own, in the form of a Python callable. Trainable modules are useful, but they do not cover all use-cases the library aims to support. Thus, the library provides three API levels which we shall explain below: (a) trainable modules, as we just seen; (b) basis modules, which cache tensors to avoid their recomputation but have no trainable parameters; (c) a fully functional API, akin to torch.nn.functional . The fully functional API, as its name suggests, consists of pure functions that have no state. Below is an example: ⬇ import torchcurves . functional as tcf bspl_func = tcf . bspline_curves ( inputs , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs , # (C, P, D) coefficients of C B-Spline functions having P coefficients in D dimensions knots , # B-Spline knots. unif. spaced in [-1, 1] with not-a-knot conditions, if unspecified. degree =5 # the piecewise-polynomial degree. 3 if unspecified. ) leg_func = tcf . legendre_curves ( inputs , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs , # (C, P, D) coefficients of C legendre polynomials having P coefficinets in D dimensions degree =50 # the polynomial degree. We always have P=degree-1. These are useful if the coefficients are not learned directly, but come as an output of another module. Note, that in case of B-Spline functions, the connection between the number of knots and the number of coefficients P must be 𝙿 = | 𝚔𝚗𝚘𝚝𝚜 | − 𝚍𝚎𝚐𝚛𝚎𝚎 + 1 \mathtt{P}=|\mathtt{knots}|-\mathtt{degree}+1 . If the knot vector is not specified, the number of uniformly-spaced knots is automatically determined from the degree and the number of coefficients P . Finally, in between learnable modules and fully functional API we have the basis modules. A basis module is similar to the functional API, but stores immutable buffers, such as the knot vector, for convenience. That way, if a model is moved from CPU to an accelerator, such as a GPU, the buffer automatically moves with it by PyTorch. Below is an example: ⬇ import torchcurves as tc # quadratic splines with 50 B-Spline functions and a rational mapping to [-1, 1] bspl_basis = tc . BSplineBasis ( degree =2, knot_config =50, input_map = ”real.rational” ) # evaluate a B-Spline function. Note - 50 coefficients for our 50 B-Spline functions. bspl_func = bspl_basis ( input , # (B, C) - a batch of input points for each curve coefs # (C, 50, D) - the coefficients of C B-Spline functions in D dimensions. ) 3.2 Applications One of the first applications that comes to mind is producing embeddings for continuous features, such as height, weight, BMI, the time since the last visit of the user on our website, and others. Imagine we have a model whose inputs are embedding vectors, such as a Factorization Machine, or a Transformer. For discrete, or categorical features - we can just map features to embeddings using a standard embedding table. But for a continuous value, we need a mapping of the value to a vector in the embedding space - and a curve is such a mapping. Here is an example that uses Legendre polynomial basis for such curves: ⬇ from torch import nn , cat import torchcurves as tc class Net ( nn . Module ): ”” ”Composes ␣ PyTorch ␣ ‘nn.Embedding‘ ␣ and ␣ Legendre ␣ curves ␣ with ␣ another ␣ model” ”” def __init__ ( self , n_discrete , n_continuous , degree , dim ): super (). __init__ () self . discrete = nn . Embedding ( n_discrete , dim ) self . cont = tc . LegendreCurve ( n_continuous , dim , degree ) self . inner_model = my_super_duper_transformer () def forward ( self , cat , cont ): # concatenate all embeddings into one tensor embeddings = cat (( self . discrete ( cat ), self . cont ( cont )), dim =-2) # invoke our desired model on the embeddings return self . inner_model ( embeddings ) Kolmogorov-Arnold networks are also an immediate application - each layer computes many univariate functions of the input, and sums-up their results. Recalling that the output of our curve layers has the shape (sample, curve, dimension) , a KAN layer just applies our curve layer, followed by a sum over the curve dimension. For convenience, we include the Sum module in the library as well. Here is an example: ⬇ from torch import nn import torchcurves as tc kan = nn . Sequential ([ # layer 1 tc . BSplineCurve ( input_dim , hidden_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), # layer 2 tc . BSplineCurve ( hidden_dim , hidden_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), # layer 3 tc . BSplineCurve ( hidden_dim , output_dim ), tc . Sum ( dim =-2), ]) A less trivial application is that of functional regression - a model whose output is itself a function. In theory, we can think of any model f ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) f({\bm{x}}) as ”functional regression” - just partition 𝒙 = ( 𝒙 1 , 𝒙 2 ) {\bm{x}}=({\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}) and define the model as the function f ⁡ ( 𝒙 1 , ⋅ ) f({\bm{x}}_{1},\cdot) . The point is not in the model’s architecture, but as the study of the model, including its performance, as such a function. Since the authors come from the online advertising field, one prominent example is fitting the probability of winning an ad auction given auction features and a non-negative bid. See Pan et al. (2020) ; Zhou et al. (2021) . Note that this is a CDF - it must be nondecreasing. A natural choice is using the property of B-Spline functions - if the coefficient vector is non-decreasing, so is the function. So below is such an example - we encode the auction into a non-decreasing vector of coefficients, which in turn serves as the coefficient vector of a B-Spline function of the bid. So below is a model for learning such a probability: ⬇ from torch import nn import torch . nn . functional as F import torchcurves as tc class AuctionWinModel ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self ): super (). __init__ () self . encoder = MySuperBestAuctionEncoder () self . spline = tc . BSplineBasis ( input_map = ”nonneg.arctan” ) def forward ( self , auction_features , bids ): # encode auction to a latent vector raw = self . encoder ( auction_features ) # convert the latent vector to non-decreasing coefficients: # use first component as is, add cumulative sum of softplus(rest) increments = F . softplus ( raw [:, 1:]) coefficients = raw [:, :1] + F . pad ( increments . cumsum (-1), (1, 0)) # non-decreasing spline function of bids to produce P(win) logits. return self . spline ( bids [ None ], coefficients […, None ]). flatten () 4 Algorithms Beyond being vectorized, the implementations we use should also be fairly efficient to be useful for machine learning research. Our efficiency goals are modest - we aim for the best we can achieve using pure PyTorch code, without custom kernels. Thus, we implement vectorized versions of well-known algorithms, both for B-Spline and Legendre polynomial evaluation. The main feature of the B-Spline basis is its sparsity - at any given point, only 𝚍𝚎𝚐𝚛𝚎𝚎 + 2 \mathtt{degree}+2 basis functions are non-zero. An efficient algorithm for exploiting the sparsity is the well-known Cox-deBoor method ( COX, 1972 ; De Boor, 1972 ) . The algorithm provides both an efficient sparsity-exploiting way to compute the value and the derivative. These, in turn, are used in a custom PyTorch autograd function to facilitate efficient back-propagation through the inputs and the coefficients. The implementation is done in a vectorized manner without iterating on any of the input dimension, but does require iterating on the degree. Thus, a spline of degree five does require six Python iterations to compute. For Legendre polynomials we have the well-known Clenshaw recursion ( Clenshaw, 1955 ) . Here, as well, we do not iterate on any input tensor dimensions, but we do iterate on the degree. Since typically good approximation is achieved with high-degree polynomials, higher than B-Splines, this may be less efficient in some situations. For example, a polynomial of degree 50 will require 51 Python for-loop iterations. In our implementation we do take special care to avoid memory allocation of tensors. We do not claim optimality, but merely a best-effort. Again, our efficiency claim is modest - to be fast enough to be useful. The library is thoroughly tested, and in particular, the results are compared to SciPy ( Virtanen et al., 2020 ) splines and NumPy ( Harris et al., 2020 ) Legendre polynomials. Derivatives are validated using internal gradient-checking mechanisms of PyTorch, that compare numerically approximated derivatives to those of back-propagation. Comparisons were done for both 32 and 64 bit floating point numbers. 5 Experiments Our objective here is giving the reader a qualitative understanding of what we mean by ”our efficiency claim is modest”. To that end, we perform two comparisons: (a) speed of inference-only computation of Legendre polynomials and Splines on CPU, compared to NumPy and SciPy; and (b) training speed of a KAN, compared to EfficientKAN ( Cao, 2024 ) , both on CPU and GPU, each implemented in its idiomatic form. Our aim is not to outperform specialized implementations, but to show that the flexibility of treating curves as general-purpose trainable primitives remains computationally practical, even when composing them into higher-level architectures such as KANs. All measurements were done on a Lenovo P14s Gen-7 laptop, with an Intel Core Ultra 7 356H CPU, and a NVIDIA RTX PRO 500 Blackwell GPU. The experiments were running on Ubuntu 26.04.01, with Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5.4, SciPy 1.18.1, and PyTorch 2.15 (CUDA 13.2). CPU affinity is limited to the first cores 1-4, which are the performance cores of that CPU, to both allow PyTorch exploit parallelism and obtain consistent speed measurements. We note that both NumPy and SciPy do not provide an autograd mechanism, thus they are by definition “inference-only” libraries. Therefore, our comparison in (a) are inference-only in nature - we perform no backpropagation, but only compute the value of the spline / Legendre polynomial functions using each library, and compare the number of milliseconds per call for various coefficient counts, curve dimensions, curve counts, and batch sizes. The results are in Figures 2 and 3 . We can see that torchcurves is slower for small number of curves or small batch sizes, and in the ballpark or faster for larger scales. It is our conjecture that at smaller scales Python overhead wins, whereas for larger scales vectorized PyTorch code lets it exploit multiple cores, while NumPy and SciPy remain serial.
