items.content: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents Megha Srivastava megha@cs.stanford.edu † † thanks: Work done during an internship at Genesis Molecular AI. Affiliation: Stanford University Michael H. Lim mlim@genesis.ml Affiliation: Genesis Molecular AI Allison M. Keys allikeys@genesis.ml Affiliation: Genesis Molecular AI Pranav Murugan pranav@genesis.ml Affiliation: Genesis Molecular AI Nate Gruver ngruver@genesis.ml Affiliation: Genesis Molecular AI Abstract Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite , a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein–ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep , a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein–ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner , which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer , which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools. Code : https://github.com/genesistherapeutics/pyrite Dataset : https://huggingface.co/datasets/genesisml/pyrite 1 Introduction Structure-based drug design typically begins from an experimental crystal structure, but because new structures are slow and costly to obtain, the field relies on computational pocket discovery, docking, and scoring ( Batool et al., 2019 ) . State-of-the-art cofolding models ( Abramson et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Genesis Research Team et al., 2025 ) , combined with diversity-promoting sampling, can now predict many plausible binding modes for a protein-ligand pair. However, this diversity is only useful if the most plausible poses can be identified. At test time, the true binding mode is unknown, and chemists must triage large sets of predictions. Errors in pose ranking can waste downstream effort and erode trust in the underlying models. We study whether agentic AI systems offer a potential path toward faster and more accurate pose ranking. Pose ranking is difficult because the available signals are individually weak and often disagree. Physics-based scores such as MM-GBSA ( Genheden and Ryde, 2015 ) , an estimate of binding free energy, and ligand torsional strain from Mogul ( Bruno et al., 2004a ) each correlate only loosely with distance to the native pose, and for a given pair they may favor different candidates. Chemists resolve these conflicts using domain knowledge, such as familiarity with the target or chemical series, and by inspecting structures in 3D visualization software. For AI agents, this highlights a central challenge: invoking tools is easy, but interpreting their conflicting outputs to reach a sound decision is not. Can a language model-based agent, given the same computational tools as a chemist, rank poses more accurately than either the tools alone or expert chemists? In this work, we create and publicly release Pyrite , the first dedicated benchmark for pairwise pose ranking of protein–ligand complexes. The limited pose diversity of many publicly available cofolding models reduces the utility of physics-based scores for ranking and provides less challenging decoys for benchmarking (Figure 2 ). This is consistent with recent work ( Khiari et al., 2026 ) , which combines an LLM agent with physicochemical tools to rank poses from classical docking, but only matches, rather than exceeds, the underlying scoring function’s accuracy on a small benchmark. In contrast, Pyrite draws poses from our proprietary cofolding model and diversity-promoting sampling algorithm, yielding a challenging benchmark of 1,500 pose pairs spanning 285 structures and 1,799 unique poses. We use Pyrite to investigate whether LLM-based agents can effectively interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools. Surprisingly, expert chemists perform near or below random chance despite substantial agreement between annotators, suggesting that conventional chemical intuition can be misleading when distinguishing high-quality cofolded poses. To systematically evaluate automated approaches, we next develop two complementary LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner directly compares candidate poses through explicit text-based chemical reasoning, while PyriteFeaturizer uses an LLM to discover informative structural features for a lightweight logistic-regression classifier. This distinction allows us to investigate whether LLMs are more effective as direct pose-ranking agents or as feature engineers for conventional statistical models. Finally we explore whether reinforcement learning (RL) can improve the pose-ranking capabilities of open-weight models. Our contributions include: 1. Pyrite , a challenging pairwise pose-ranking benchmark constructed from diverse, high-quality cofolded poses. We find that expert chemists perform near or below random chance, despite substantial inter-annotator agreement, and that conventional physics-based scores can be anti-correlated with correctness. 2. PyriteRep , a structured data format for representing 3D poses, including molecular geometry, protein–ligand interactions, and precomputed physicochemical features. We demonstrate that PyriteRep substantially improves LLM-based agents’ pose-ranking accuracy compared to raw 3D coordinates alone. 3. PyriteReasoner , an LLM-based agent that directly ranks pose pairs through text-based chemical reasoning, achieving up to 67% accuracy. RL improves the performance of open-weight models, narrowing the gap with closed-source frontier models. 4. PyriteFeaturizer , an LLM-based coding agent that discovers and implements predictive structural features for a simple logistic-regression classifier. By combining code-derived quantitative descriptors with features generated through LLM subcalls, PyriteFeaturizer achieves up to 74% pose-ranking accuracy, the highest performance on our benchmark. RL substantially improves feature discovery in open-weight models, enabling them to match or exceed closed-source frontier models. Overall, our results demonstrate that ranking poses generated by modern cofolding models remains a challenging task, even for experienced chemists. While classical models trained on quantitative structural features are surprisingly competitive with direct LLM reasoning, LLM-guided feature discovery offers a promising way to improve upon these models by incorporating additional chemical and biological knowledge. Figure 1: Interface for human expert annotations on our pairwise pose ranking benchmark Pyrite (ground truth crystal shown only for paper visualization). The example shows two predicted poses of a potential small-molecule inhibitor of the autotaxin protein ( Protein Data Bank 7G63 ), with toggle control for 2D contact map and interactive 3D and overlay views. Experts are asked to select which pose is closer to the crystallographic binding mode (selecting 1-5), write factors in favor of both pose A and B, and describe their reasoning on how they weigh these factors for pose selection. Annotators are also provided MM-GBSA scores and the # of unusual torsions using Mogul for each pose. 2 Problem Setup: Pose Ranking To introduce the pose ranking problem, let us walk through the example in Figure 1 , which shows two predicted poses (Poses A and B) of a small-molecule that binds to autotaxin protein ( Protein Data Bank 7G63 ). These predictions come from a proprietary cofolding model. At test time, the ground truth crystallographic binding mode of the protein-ligand complex is unknown; therefore, a strong pose ranker should be able to select which pose is closer to the ground truth 3D structure. In the example shown, the correct choice is Pose A. Now, consider the following reasoning from an expert chemist: Expert Reasoning: Both poses are governed almost exclusively by hydrophobic/aromatic interactions of a mostly flat, conjugated system. Pose A seems a bit more buried. The pyridine could rotate to form the same H-bond with Lys 648 as in Pose B. The chemist weighs many different factors before ultimately choosing Pose A, combining physical reasoning with more intuitive features. Our goal is to learn a strong pose ranker, and investigate whether AI agents based on language models can successfully reason over the outputs of computational chemistry tools to achieve high pose ranking accuracy. Although strong pairwise pose ranking ability is not the same as overall ranking, both tasks share the same underlying reasoning requirements from AI agents. We specifically chose to focus on a pairwise pose ranking due to its simplicity in light of context-length limits of language models, as well as the cognitive burden placed on the human experts we use for evaluating our benchmark. Furthermore, pairwise comparison allows us to derive better semantic features than scoring a single pose. 2.1 Representing poses for AI agents with PyriteRep Inspired by recent work showing that molecular graph schemas help improve the performance of LLM-based systems for chemical discovery ( Runcie et al., 2026 ) , we introduce PyriteRep , a structured data format for representing 3D poses for our pose ranking task. In Section B , we will show that PyriteRep improves the performance of LLM-based agents reasoning in text over pose ranking, in comparison to only providing each pose’s 3D-coordinates. PyriteRep consists of 29 features, including both pose-invariant (identical for both poses) and pose-dependent features. These features are the outputs of several computational chemistry tools, including RDKit and OpenMM ( Landrum et al., 2026 ; Eastman et al., 2024 ) . We describe the features in the boxes below. MM-GBSA Score : Binding energy score, estimated from first step of docking pipeline. 3 Pyrite Benchmark Creation Figure 2: Top-k pose enrichment and diversity across cofolding models For each of Boltz2, Protenix, ESMFold2, and our cofolding model, we scored 120 poses per complex against the ground truth crystal, calling a pose a "hit" at RMSD < 2 Å and lDDT-PLI ≥ \geq 0.8. Top Row shows top-k enrichment (EF@k = hits in the top-k over hits expected at random, pooled across complexes, so random = 1). Middle Row and Bottom Row : the 3rd-party cofolding models are far less diverse than ours, measured both by the distribution of per-pair RMSD and Interaction IoU. 3.1 Generating Diverse Poses We create Pyrite using poses from our proprietary cofolding model and inference-time method that generates a diverse set of binding poses for each target, while using physics-based guidance to steer predictions toward chemically and geometrically valid structures. Figure 2 shows that the poses from our model are more diverse than three different public 3rd-party models (Boltz2 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) , Protenix ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and ESMFold2 ( Candido et al., 2026 ) ). Moreover, for all three cofolding models, both the model’s own confidence and MM-GBSA score barely passes random chance at pose ranking, falling significantly short of the oracle. Only our system receives real enrichment from MM-GBSA, but that underperforms a far higher ceiling, necessitating building stronger pose-ranking methods. To create our benchmark, we first use our cofolding model to sample up to 120 poses for protein-ligand queries spanning more than 50,000 structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (2026) . We then take the top-25 poses scored by MM-GBSA for each query, entering a tight regime of high-quality poses where, as we will later show in Figure 2 , MM-GBSA can actually become anti-correlated with pose ranking performance. We then consider all possible pairs of poses for the same query, and filter this set to create Pyrite . 3.2 Filtering Pose Pairs for Comparison Not all pairs are useful for a pose ranking benchmark: for example, some poses may be obviously low quality or structurally invalid, while some pairs of poses might be too similar to each other to distinguish. We first categorize each pose by measuring RMSD-to-ground truth crystal over the 3D coordinates for each atom, lDDT-PLI (Local Distance Difference Test for Protein–Ligand Interactions), which is a scoring metric that measures local interatomic distances ( Robin et al., 2023 ) , and the interaction recall given the reference crystal’s interactions. We designate thresholds for these metrics in order to create three categories: Pose Categorization (Ground Truth Crystal Reference) 1. GOOD : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 1 Å, lDDT-PLI ≥ 0.85 \geq 0.85 , interaction recall ≥ 0.90 \geq 0.90 2. MAYBE : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 2 Å and ≥ \geq 1 Å, 0.5 ≤ 0.5\leq lDDT-PLI < 0.85 <0.85 3. BAD : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 4 Å and ≥ 2 \geq 2 Å, lDDT-PLI < 0.5 <0.5 , interaction recall < 0.5 <0.5 We filter down our dataset to only consist of Hard pairs (GOOD, MAYBE) and Easy pairs (GOOD, BAD), ensuring that every pair in Pyrite consists of at least one high-quality pose. However, we found that this high-level categorization was not sufficient in removing pairs with poses that were too similar or low-quality, so we introduced additional filtering conditions described in Appendix A . After applying all these filters, our final Pyrite benchmark consists of 1,500 pose pairs spanning 285 unique structures and 1,799 unique poses. Of these structures, 195 were released in the RCSB Protein Data Bank before September 30, 2021 ( pre-AF3 ) and 90 were released afterwards ( post-AF3 ). Because human annotation is costly, we select a curated subset of 750 pairs (177 structures, 890 poses), on which we collect annotations from expert chemists (see Section 4 ). For the rest of this paper, we will focus on three splits within Pyrite : • pre-AF3 curated : 485 pairs, 121 structures. We report human accuracy on this split in Section 4 . We do not evaluate LLM agents (see Sections 6.1 and 6.3 ) on pre-AF3 pairs, since we reserve the pre-AF3 data for training data • post-AF3 all : 484 pairs, 90 structures, every post-AF3 pair in Pyrite . • post-AF3 curated : 265 pairs, 56 structures, the subset of post-AF3 all with human annotations. This is the only split where we can directly compare LLM agents against expert chemists. Because Pyrite is a balanced binary-classification task, we focus on comparing the accuracy of various pose-ranking methods. To ensure fair comparison, we treat abstentions (neither choosing Pose A or B) as incorrect across all methods. 3.3 Physics scores are anti-correlated for strong pose decoys We first check whether the pre-computed physics scores we include in PyriteRep (see Section 2.1 ) can, as individual features, serve a strong pose rankers on Pyrite . For example, the MM-GBSA score estimates the binding free energy of a protein-ligand complex by combining molecular mechanics energies with implicit solvation models; intuitively, a lower MM-GBSA structure can imply that the predicted pose is more thermodynamically stable and closer to the native binding mode. However, we find that selecting the pose with the lower MM-GBSA score is anti-correlated with the correct choice in Pyrite (see Table 1 ), leading to low accuracy. This is likely due to Pyrite consisting of high-quality pose decoys that are predicted to be thermodynamically stable by construction, and therefore MM-GBSA is not a reliable score for pose ranking in this regime. In fact, Figure 2 shows no ranking improvement when k < 25, and a slight dip in the k < 10 regime of enrichment scores when using MM-GBSA for ranking poses from our system. Importantly, no aspect of our benchmark creation intentionally selected for pose pairs where MM-GBSA provided an incorrect signal; rather, this appears to be a property of the high-quality pose regime for cofolding. Table 1 shows that other scores, including the total # \# of interactions, total torsion strain, and total # \# of unusual torsion angles using Mogul, similarly result in poor pose ranking accuracy across all splits. Collectively, these results suggest that any strong pose ranking method needs to both (i) overcome any potential inductive biases (e.g. that lower MM-GBSA scores are more favorable), and (ii) learn non-trivial ways to combine all the features in PyriteRep . Given these results, a natural question is whether one should simply invert the sign of a physical score like MM-GBSA to use as the ranking criterion, which would by construction achieve above-chance accuracy on Pyrite . This would be problematic as such a rule contradicts the physical interpretation of the score, and would be inadvisable to deploy without evidence that the inversion generalizes beyond our benchmark: in fact, Figure 2 shows that the relationship between MM-GBSA and pose correctness depends on the number of candidate poses retained. Nevertheless, we find empirically that our trained methods presented later in Section 6 outperform sign-flipped MM-GBSA with a low agreement-rate (Appendix G ), indicating that it is possible to learn a stronger decision rule that is not just a noisy copy of inverted physical heuristics. We next evaluate Pyrite with expert human chemists. Although our initial goal was to use the reasoning text provided by human experts to guide the design a strong automated pose-ranking method, we surprisingly find that expert chemists perform below/at random chance on Pyrite , as we describe below. 4.1 Human expert annotation overview We recruit 5 expert chemists with an average of more than 10 years of experience with computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), molecular docking, and virtual screening. Each annotator was provided a set of pose pairs, and asked to choose which pose (A or B) is closer to the crystallographic binding mode for each pair, providing the following: 1. Selection : A choice from 1-5 corresponding to which pose the expert believes is closer to the crystallographic binding mode (1: Pose A clearly better, 2: Pose A slightly better, 3: About the same, 4: Pose B slightly better, 5: Pose B clearly better). 2. Factors favoring Pose A/B: Any specific factors (or "None") about both Pose A and B that make it closer to the crystallographic binding mode. 3. Overall Reasoning : The overall reasoning behind the selection, describing all features of the two poses that influenced your decision, as well as any trade-offs. For the reasoning, we enforce a minimum 150 character requirement. Figure 1 shows the interface provided to human experts, as well as example annotations. Experts were provided both 3D visualizations and 2D contact maps, as well as two physics-based and statistical scores: MM-GBSA and Mogul # of Unusual Torsions. Furthermore, experts were provided the UniProt protein family name and description, and could download PDB/SDF files of the protein-ligand poses to further analyze in molecular visuali

Overall, our results demonstrate that ranking poses generated by modern cofolding models remains a challenging task, even for experienced chemists. While classical models trained on quantitative structural features are surprisingly competitive with direct LLM reasoning, LLM-guided feature discovery offers a promising way to improve upon these models by incorporating additional chemical and biological knowledge. Figure 1: Interface for human expert annotations on our pairwise pose ranking benchmark Pyrite (ground truth crystal shown only for paper visualization). The example shows two predicted poses of a potential small-molecule inhibitor of the autotaxin protein ( Protein Data Bank 7G63 ), with toggle control for 2D contact map and interactive 3D and overlay views. Experts are asked to select which pose is closer to the crystallographic binding mode (selecting 1-5), write factors in favor of both pose A and B, and describe their reasoning on how they weigh these factors for pose selection. Annotators are also provided MM-GBSA scores and the # of unusual torsions using Mogul for each pose. 2 Problem Setup: Pose Ranking To introduce the pose ranking problem, let us walk through the example in Figure 1 , which shows two predicted poses (Poses A and B) of a small-molecule that binds to autotaxin protein ( Protein Data Bank 7G63 ). These predictions come from a proprietary cofolding model. At test time, the ground truth crystallographic binding mode of the protein-ligand complex is unknown; therefore, a strong pose ranker should be able to select which pose is closer to the ground truth 3D structure. In the example shown, the correct choice is Pose A. Now, consider the following reasoning from an expert chemist: Expert Reasoning: Both poses are governed almost exclusively by hydrophobic/aromatic interactions of a mostly flat, conjugated system. Pose A seems a bit more buried. The pyridine could rotate to form the same H-bond with Lys 648 as in Pose B. The chemist weighs many different factors before ultimately choosing Pose A, combining physical reasoning with more intuitive features. Our goal is to learn a strong pose ranker, and investigate whether AI agents based on language models can successfully reason over the outputs of computational chemistry tools to achieve high pose ranking accuracy. Although strong pairwise pose ranking ability is not the same as overall ranking, both tasks share the same underlying reasoning requirements from AI agents. We specifically chose to focus on a pairwise pose ranking due to its simplicity in light of context-length limits of language models, as well as the cognitive burden placed on the human experts we use for evaluating our benchmark. Furthermore, pairwise comparison allows us to derive better semantic features than scoring a single pose. 2.1 Representing poses for AI agents with PyriteRep Inspired by recent work showing that molecular graph schemas help improve the performance of LLM-based systems for chemical discovery ( Runcie et al., 2026 ) , we introduce PyriteRep , a structured data format for representing 3D poses for our pose ranking task. In Section B , we will show that PyriteRep improves the performance of LLM-based agents reasoning in text over pose ranking, in comparison to only providing each pose’s 3D-coordinates. PyriteRep consists of 29 features, including both pose-invariant (identical for both poses) and pose-dependent features. These features are the outputs of several computational chemistry tools, including RDKit and OpenMM ( Landrum et al., 2026 ; Eastman et al., 2024 ) . We describe the features in the boxes below. MM-GBSA Score : Binding energy score, estimated from first step of docking pipeline. 3 Pyrite Benchmark Creation Figure 2: Top-k pose enrichment and diversity across cofolding models For each of Boltz2, Protenix, ESMFold2, and our cofolding model, we scored 120 poses per complex against the ground truth crystal, calling a pose a "hit" at RMSD < 2 Å and lDDT-PLI ≥ \geq 0.8. Top Row shows top-k enrichment (EF@k = hits in the top-k over hits expected at random, pooled across complexes, so random = 1). Middle Row and Bottom Row : the 3rd-party cofolding models are far less diverse than ours, measured both by the distribution of per-pair RMSD and Interaction IoU. 3.1 Generating Diverse Poses We create Pyrite using poses from our proprietary cofolding model and inference-time method that generates a diverse set of binding poses for each target, while using physics-based guidance to steer predictions toward chemically and geometrically valid structures. Figure 2 shows that the poses from our model are more diverse than three different public 3rd-party models (Boltz2 ( Passaro et al., 2025 ) , Protenix ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and ESMFold2 ( Candido et al., 2026 ) ). Moreover, for all three cofolding models, both the model’s own confidence and MM-GBSA score barely passes random chance at pose ranking, falling significantly short of the oracle. Only our system receives real enrichment from MM-GBSA, but that underperforms a far higher ceiling, necessitating building stronger pose-ranking methods. To create our benchmark, we first use our cofolding model to sample up to 120 poses for protein-ligand queries spanning more than 50,000 structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (2026) . We then take the top-25 poses scored by MM-GBSA for each query, entering a tight regime of high-quality poses where, as we will later show in Figure 2 , MM-GBSA can actually become anti-correlated with pose ranking performance. We then consider all possible pairs of poses for the same query, and filter this set to create Pyrite . 3.2 Filtering Pose Pairs for Comparison Not all pairs are useful for a pose ranking benchmark: for example, some poses may be obviously low quality or structurally invalid, while some pairs of poses might be too similar to each other to distinguish. We first categorize each pose by measuring RMSD-to-ground truth crystal over the 3D coordinates for each atom, lDDT-PLI (Local Distance Difference Test for Protein–Ligand Interactions), which is a scoring metric that measures local interatomic distances ( Robin et al., 2023 ) , and the interaction recall given the reference crystal’s interactions. We designate thresholds for these metrics in order to create three categories: Pose Categorization (Ground Truth Crystal Reference) 1. GOOD : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 1 Å, lDDT-PLI ≥ 0.85 \geq 0.85 , interaction recall ≥ 0.90 \geq 0.90 2. MAYBE : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 2 Å and ≥ \geq 1 Å, 0.5 ≤ 0.5\leq lDDT-PLI < 0.85 <0.85 3. BAD : RMSD-to-ground truth crystal < 4 Å and ≥ 2 \geq 2 Å, lDDT-PLI < 0.5 <0.5 , interaction recall < 0.5 <0.5 We filter down our dataset to only consist of Hard pairs (GOOD, MAYBE) and Easy pairs (GOOD, BAD), ensuring that every pair in Pyrite consists of at least one high-quality pose. However, we found that this high-level categorization was not sufficient in removing pairs with poses that were too similar or low-quality, so we introduced additional filtering conditions described in Appendix A . After applying all these filters, our final Pyrite benchmark consists of 1,500 pose pairs spanning 285 unique structures and 1,799 unique poses. Of these structures, 195 were released in the RCSB Protein Data Bank before September 30, 2021 ( pre-AF3 ) and 90 were released afterwards ( post-AF3 ). Because human annotation is costly, we select a curated subset of 750 pairs (177 structures, 890 poses), on which we collect annotations from expert chemists (see Section 4 ). For the rest of this paper, we will focus on three splits within Pyrite : • pre-AF3 curated : 485 pairs, 121 structures. We report human accuracy on this split in Section 4 . We do not evaluate LLM agents (see Sections 6.1 and 6.3 ) on pre-AF3 pairs, since we reserve the pre-AF3 data for training data • post-AF3 all : 484 pairs, 90 structures, every post-AF3 pair in Pyrite . • post-AF3 curated : 265 pairs, 56 structures, the subset of post-AF3 all with human annotations. This is the only split where we can directly compare LLM agents against expert chemists. Because Pyrite is a balanced binary-classification task, we focus on comparing the accuracy of various pose-ranking methods. To ensure fair comparison, we treat abstentions (neither choosing Pose A or B) as incorrect across all methods. 3.3 Physics scores are anti-correlated for strong pose decoys We first check whether the pre-computed physics scores we include in PyriteRep (see Section 2.1 ) can, as individual features, serve a strong pose rankers on Pyrite . For example, the MM-GBSA score estimates the binding free energy of a protein-ligand complex by combining molecular mechanics energies with implicit solvation models; intuitively, a lower MM-GBSA structure can imply that the predicted pose is more thermodynamically stable and closer to the native binding mode. However, we find that selecting the pose with the lower MM-GBSA score is anti-correlated with the correct choice in Pyrite (see Table 1 ), leading to low accuracy. This is likely due to Pyrite consisting of high-quality pose decoys that are predicted to be thermodynamically stable by construction, and therefore MM-GBSA is not a reliable score for pose ranking in this regime. In fact, Figure 2 shows no ranking improvement when k < 25, and a slight dip in the k < 10 regime of enrichment scores when using MM-GBSA for ranking poses from our system. Importantly, no aspect of our benchmark creation intentionally selected for pose pairs where MM-GBSA provided an incorrect signal; rather, this appears to be a property of the high-quality pose regime for cofolding. Table 1 shows that other scores, including the total # \# of interactions, total torsion strain, and total # \# of unusual torsion angles using Mogul, similarly result in poor pose ranking accuracy across all splits. Collectively, these results suggest that any strong pose ranking method needs to both (i) overcome any potential inductive biases (e.g. that lower MM-GBSA scores are more favorable), and (ii) learn non-trivial ways to combine all the features in PyriteRep . Given these results, a natural question is whether one should simply invert the sign of a physical score like MM-GBSA to use as the ranking criterion, which would by construction achieve above-chance accuracy on Pyrite . This would be problematic as such a rule contradicts the physical interpretation of the score, and would be inadvisable to deploy without evidence that the inversion generalizes beyond our benchmark: in fact, Figure 2 shows that the relationship between MM-GBSA and pose correctness depends on the number of candidate poses retained. Nevertheless, we find empirically that our trained methods presented later in Section 6 outperform sign-flipped MM-GBSA with a low agreement-rate (Appendix G ), indicating that it is possible to learn a stronger decision rule that is not just a noisy copy of inverted physical heuristics. Table 1: Accuracy and 95% CIs from expert chemists, Boltz-2 confidence, and various physics scores from PyriteRep across three benchmark splits. No method achieves pairwise accuracy significantly above chance. We next evaluate Pyrite with expert human chemists. Although our initial goal was to use the reasoning text provided by human experts to guide the design a strong automated pose-ranking method, we surprisingly find that expert chemists perform below/at random chance on Pyrite , as we describe below. 4.1 Human expert annotation overview We recruit 5 expert chemists with an average of more than 10 years of experience with computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), molecular docking, and virtual screening. Each annotator was provided a set of pose pairs, and asked to choose which pose (A or B) is closer to the crystallographic binding mode for each pair, providing the following: 1. Selection : A choice from 1-5 corresponding to which pose the expert believes is closer to the crystallographic binding mode (1: Pose A clearly better, 2: Pose A slightly better, 3: About the same, 4: Pose B slightly better, 5: Pose B clearly better). 2. Factors favoring Pose A/B: Any specific factors (or "None") about both Pose A and B that make it closer to the crystallographic binding mode. 3. Overall Reasoning : The overall reasoning behind the selection, describing all features of the two poses that influenced your decision, as well as any trade-offs. For the reasoning, we enforce a minimum 150 character requirement. Figure 1 shows the interface provided to human experts, as well as example annotations. Experts were provided both 3D visualizations and 2D contact maps, as well as two physics-based and statistical scores: MM-GBSA and Mogul # of Unusual Torsions. Furthermore, experts were provided the UniProt protein family name and description, and could download PDB/SDF files of the protein-ligand poses to further analyze in molecular visuali

items.content: ReTrace : Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows Kaiyuan Hou † † thanks: Work done during an internship at Amazon. † † thanks: Equal Contribution Affiliation: Columbia University Email: kh3119@columbia.edu Yang Ping Kuo 2 2 footnotemark: 2 † † thanks: Corresponding Author Affiliation: Amazon Email: yangkuo@amazon.com Indranil Bhattacharya 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Amazon Email: bindrani@amazon.com Rohith Nama 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Amazon Email: rohinama@amazon.com Arushi Gupta 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Amazon Email: arushimg@amazon.com Carlos D. Castillo Affiliation: Amazon Email: cdcast@amazon.com Prathap Ramachandra Affiliation: Amazon Email: prathara@amazon.com Xiaofan Jiang Affiliation: Columbia University Email: jiang@ee.columbia.edu Francesco Carbone Affiliation: Amazon Email: carbonef@amazon.com Abstract Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace , which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent’s reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On 79 79 procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach 93.8 % 93.8\% completion, against 96.8 % 96.8\% for the agent, at 24 % 24\% lower cost per task. On τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench , they reach 75.8 % 75.8\% task success (agent: 80.6 % 80.6\% ) and run in 1.3 1.3 s instead of 170 170 s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift k = 2 k{=}2 workflows from 66.7 % 66.7\% to 81.2 % 81.2\% . On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ( 80.6 % 80.6\% vs. 83.6 % 83.6\% ), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to 87.8 % 87.8\% at 0.40 0.40 s per task, compared to 85.5 % 85.5\% in 46.6 46.6 s for the agent. 1 Introduction Many business processes run thousands of times on different inputs: a support case is triaged, a form is checked, an order is escalated. Automating such a process has traditionally meant building a workflow by hand, wiring tools, inputs, and branches in code or in a workflow editor ( Object Management Group, 2011 ; van der Aalst et al., 2018 ) . Large Language Model (LLM) agents remove most of this effort. A process owner writes a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in natural language, and the agent reads it and calls the available tools ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Nandi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . The price is paid at run time: the agent calls an LLM to plan, route, and transform data at every step of every execution, which is slow and expensive at high volume. Figure 1 : From agent runs to executable workflows. The agent, and methods that reuse its past runs as examples or memory, call an LLM to choose each step. ReTrace turns the agent’s reasoning and tool calls into rules before deployment; at run time, code selects the next step. These costs are visible in production. Of the 5,115 5{,}115 automations that customers created on our enterprise business process automation platform between April and June 2026, 91.8 % 91.8\% were agents that plan at run time, yet seven of the ten most frequently executed automations were fixed workflows. For agents using three to five tools, choosing the next step took 37 37 – 43 % 43\% of execution time, on top of the token cost. For a procedure that runs often, building a workflow once pays off: from the measured savings and a τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench construction cost, we estimate that construction is recovered after about 75 75 executions, while each of those seven workflows ran 297 297 k– 528 528 k times in three months (Appendix L ). Logged agent runs, or traces , show how a procedure is carried out, and prior work reuses them as written guidance, skills, or code ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang and Lu, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Replacing the agent with a workflow, however, requires knowing when each tool should be called and where each of its inputs comes from. Tool calls alone often do not say. If an agent looks up an order and then escalates to a human, the trace does not show whether the shipping status caused the escalation. The agent’s reasoning often does, and it can also mention alternatives that no logged run took. Giving a model more raw traces is not enough: with many long traces, the workflow generator eventually writes worse code (Section 5.1 ). We present ReTrace , which builds a reusable workflow from an SOP and agent traces that include reasoning (Figure 1 ). It extracts the condition, tool, and input sources behind each step, merges them across traces into a compact rule document that links every rule to its evidence, and generates an executable workflow from that document. LLMs are used only in this one-time construction; at run time, code selects the next step, though a tool may still call a model, for example to classify a document. Our contributions are: • Rules from agent reasoning. We combine the agent’s reasoning with its tool records to recover action conditions, input sources, and alternatives that no logged run executed. • One rule document, several platforms. Only the final stage depends on the target, so the same pipeline yields Python code for two public benchmarks and typed workflow graphs for our production platform. • Evidence from production and two public benchmarks. On 79 79 production procedures and on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench , ReTrace workflows come within 3 3 and 5 5 points of the agent, respectively, while cutting enterprise cost per task by 24 % 24\% and τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench time per task from 170 170 s to 1.3 1.3 s. Removing the agent’s reasoning costs 8.8 8.8 and 6.2 6.2 points, respectively, and gains 1.7 1.7 on SOP-Bench. Repaired workflows reach 81.2 % 81.2\% on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench (agent: 80.6 % 80.6\% , n.s.) and 87.8 % 87.8\% on SOP-Bench (agent: 85.5 % 85.5\% ), where unrepaired ReTrace trails few-shot. 2 Related Work Reusing agent experience. Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) stores workflow descriptions as written guidance for an agent, while ExpeL and ReasoningBank store lessons and strategies ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) . Voyager, ASI, SKILL-DISCO, and NSI instead produce reusable code, or skills, that an LLM agent selects and calls at run time ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) . Skill Factory builds skills from successful runs, but a model still picks a skill and fills its inputs for each task ( Wang and Lu, 2026 ) ; BPOP learns only which actions must precede others ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In all of these but BPOP, a model keeps choosing steps; ReTrace compiles conditions and input sources into a workflow that does not need one. SOP benchmarks test whether an agent follows a written procedure at run time ( Li et al., 2025 ; Nandi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ; ReTrace instead compiles the procedure once, so no agent has to follow it on each run. Compiling executable workflows. TraceCompiler tracks how tool outputs feed later inputs and builds mostly deterministic workflows that may still call an LLM to fill some inputs; on AppWorld, it escalates when a required branch never appeared in the logged runs ( El Yadouni and Li, 2026 ) . Trace2Policy reconstructs experts’ decision rules from behavior records with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) and revises them on validation errors; its deployed version is human-refined Python that runs without an LLM ( Zha et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench keeps a model in the loop at run time: PLVR guides or checks a small model that still generates actions, and STAGE runs model-backed judgment nodes inside a code-controlled graph ( Bhat et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . ReTrace differs in its evidence: it reads the conditions and alternatives stated in the agent’s own reasoning, which can cover branches that no logged run took. Workflow search and optimization methods tune agent designs, prompts, or LLM-calling steps ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhuge et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Khattab et al., 2024 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) ; we instead recover workflow rules from an SOP and logged runs. Table 10 in Appendix K compares the closest methods. 3 Method 3.1 Inputs and target workflow A task family is a set of inputs handled by the same SOP P P , for example support cases under one troubleshooting procedure. We use k k traces 𝒯 k = { τ ( 1 ) , … , τ ( k ) } \mathcal{T}_{k}=\{\tau^{(1)},\dots,\tau^{(k)}\} of an agent on such inputs. A trace τ = ( s 1 , … , s L ) \tau=(s_{1},\dots,s_{L}) records each of its L L steps as s t = ( r t , a t , v t , o t ) s_{t}=(r_{t},a_{t},v_{t},o_{t}) , where r t r_{t} is the agent’s reasoning for the step, a t a_{t} the tool called, v t v_{t} its inputs, and o t o_{t} the result. The output is an executable workflow π \pi , built once per procedure and reused on new inputs. At run time, code chooses the next step without calling an LLM; this is what we mean by planner-free . Individual tools may still call models. The workflow is Python code on the public benchmarks and a typed graph of steps on Internal , our enterprise dataset. 3.2 Building the workflow Construction has three stages: extraction reads each step, aggregation merges evidence across traces into an Intermediate Representation (IR) ℐ \mathcal{I} (a compact rule document); synthesis generates the workflow from it. Algorithm 1 in Appendix B gives the full procedure. Extraction: reading each step. For each step, an LLM extracts a record z t = ( g t , α t , a t , v t , ω t ) z_{t}=(g_{t},\alpha_{t},a_{t},v_{t},\omega_{t}) . The reasoning supplies the condition g t g_{t} under which the action applies and the intended action α t \alpha_{t} . The condition may use only information available before the action: “airplane mode is on” can justify turning it off, but the result of turning it off cannot. The tool record supplies the tool a t a_{t} , its typed inputs v t v_{t} , and the source ω t \omega_{t} of each input, such as a task input, an earlier result, or a constant; unknown sources are marked as such. Case-specific values, such as a customer ID, become variables filled from each new task. The record also keeps alternative actions that the reasoning mentions but the agent did not take. Aggregation: combining traces into rules. An LLM first summarizes each trace against the SOP, matching its steps to the procedure and noting alternatives that were mentioned but not executed. A merge step then combines the summaries: it unifies repeated steps, works out how earlier results feed later inputs, checks the reasoning against the recorded calls and outcomes, and resolves disagreements using the SOP, giving a reason for anything it drops. The result is a completion check and an ordered list of rules: ℐ = ( χ , ⟨ ( g 1 , α 1 ) , … , ( g m , α m ) ⟩ ) . \mathcal{I}=\big(\chi,\langle(g_{1},\alpha_{1}),\dots,(g_{m},\alpha_{m})\rangle\big). (1) Here χ \chi tests whether the task is complete, and rule j j pairs a condition, or guard , g j g_{j} with an action α j \alpha_{j} , its tool, and its input sources. The rules form a decision list ( Rivest, 1987 ) . Castillo Affiliation: Amazon Email: cdcast@amazon.com Prathap Ramachandra Affiliation: Amazon Email: prathara@amazon.com Xiaofan Jiang Affiliation: Columbia University Email: jiang@ee.columbia.edu Francesco Carbone Affiliation: Amazon Email: carbonef@amazon.com Abstract Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace , which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent’s reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On 79 79 procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach 93.8 % 93.8\% completion, against 96.8 % 96.8\% for the agent, at 24 % 24\% lower cost per task. On τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench , they reach 75.8 % 75.8\% task success (agent: 80.6 % 80.6\% ) and run in 1.3 1.3 s instead of 170 170 s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift k = 2 k{=}2 workflows from 66.7 % 66.7\% to 81.2 % 81.2\% . On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ( 80.6 % 80.6\% vs. 83.6 % 83.6\% ), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to 87.8 % 87.8\% at 0.40 0.40 s per task, compared to 85.5 % 85.5\% in 46.6 46.6 s for the agent. 1 Introduction Many business processes run thousands of times on different inputs: a support case is triaged, a form is checked, an order is escalated. Automating such a process has traditionally meant building a workflow by hand, wiring tools, inputs, and branches in code or in a workflow editor ( Object Management Group, 2011 ; van der Aalst et al., 2018 ) . Large Language Model (LLM) agents remove most of this effort. A process owner writes a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in natural language, and the agent reads it and calls the available tools ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Nandi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . The price is paid at run time: the agent calls an LLM to plan, route, and transform data at every step of every execution, which is slow and expensive at high volume. Figure 1 : From agent runs to executable workflows. The agent, and methods that reuse its past runs as examples or memory, call an LLM to choose each step. ReTrace turns the agent’s reasoning and tool calls into rules before deployment; at run time, code selects the next step. These costs are visible in production. Of the 5,115 5{,}115 automations that customers created on our enterprise business process automation platform between April and June 2026, 91.8 % 91.8\% were agents that plan at run time, yet seven of the ten most frequently executed automations were fixed workflows. For agents using three to five tools, choosing the next step took 37 37 – 43 % 43\% of execution time, on top of the token cost. For a procedure that runs often, building a workflow once pays off: from the measured savings and a τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench construction cost, we estimate that construction is recovered after about 75 75 executions, while each of those seven workflows ran 297 297 k– 528 528 k times in three months (Appendix L ). Logged agent runs, or traces , show how a procedure is carried out, and prior work reuses them as written guidance, skills, or code ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang and Lu, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Replacing the agent with a workflow, however, requires knowing when each tool should be called and where each of its inputs comes from. Tool calls alone often do not say. If an agent looks up an order and then escalates to a human, the trace does not show whether the shipping status caused the escalation. The agent’s reasoning often does, and it can also mention alternatives that no logged run took. Giving a model more raw traces is not enough: with many long traces, the workflow generator eventually writes worse code (Section 5.1 ). We present ReTrace , which builds a reusable workflow from an SOP and agent traces that include reasoning (Figure 1 ). It extracts the condition, tool, and input sources behind each step, merges them across traces into a compact rule document that links every rule to its evidence, and generates an executable workflow from that document. LLMs are used only in this one-time construction; at run time, code selects the next step, though a tool may still call a model, for example to classify a document. Our contributions are: • Rules from agent reasoning. We combine the agent’s reasoning with its tool records to recover action conditions, input sources, and alternatives that no logged run executed. • One rule document, several platforms. Only the final stage depends on the target, so the same pipeline yields Python code for two public benchmarks and typed workflow graphs for our production platform. • Evidence from production and two public benchmarks. On 79 79 production procedures and on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench , ReTrace workflows come within 3 3 and 5 5 points of the agent, respectively, while cutting enterprise cost per task by 24 % 24\% and τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench time per task from 170 170 s to 1.3 1.3 s. Removing the agent’s reasoning costs 8.8 8.8 and 6.2 6.2 points, respectively, and gains 1.7 1.7 on SOP-Bench. Repaired workflows reach 81.2 % 81.2\% on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench (agent: 80.6 % 80.6\% , n.s.) and 87.8 % 87.8\% on SOP-Bench (agent: 85.5 % 85.5\% ), where unrepaired ReTrace trails few-shot. 2 Related Work Reusing agent experience. Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) stores workflow descriptions as written guidance for an agent, while ExpeL and ReasoningBank store lessons and strategies ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) . Voyager, ASI, SKILL-DISCO, and NSI instead produce reusable code, or skills, that an LLM agent selects and calls at run time ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) . Skill Factory builds skills from successful runs, but a model still picks a skill and fills its inputs for each task ( Wang and Lu, 2026 ) ; BPOP learns only which actions must precede others ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In all of these but BPOP, a model keeps choosing steps; ReTrace compiles conditions and input sources into a workflow that does not need one. SOP benchmarks test whether an agent follows a written procedure at run time ( Li et al., 2025 ; Nandi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) ; ReTrace instead compiles the procedure once, so no agent has to follow it on each run. Compiling executable workflows. TraceCompiler tracks how tool outputs feed later inputs and builds mostly deterministic workflows that may still call an LLM to fill some inputs; on AppWorld, it escalates when a required branch never appeared in the logged runs ( El Yadouni and Li, 2026 ) . Trace2Policy reconstructs experts’ decision rules from behavior records with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) and revises them on validation errors; its deployed version is human-refined Python that runs without an LLM ( Zha et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work on τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench keeps a model in the loop at run time: PLVR guides or checks a small model that still generates actions, and STAGE runs model-backed judgment nodes inside a code-controlled graph ( Bhat et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . items.title: High-Level Platform meets in Moldova to strengthen digital connectivity between the EU, the Black Sea region, South-Caucasus and Central Asia
items.summary: On 9 and 10 November, the first High-Level Connectivity Platform Meeting on Digital took place in Chișinău, Moldova, jointly hosted by the European Commission and the Moldovan Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalisation. © Oleksii Liskonih The meeting sets the groundwork for stronger digital connectivity between Europe and Centra Asia, via the Black Sea region, the South Caucasus and Türkiye, in the form of an Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer. The Platform brings together European technology, expertise, standards and financing to strengthen secure, trusted and resilient digital connectivity. It contributes to the EU's plans to develop the Middle Corridor, which will connect Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and directly to the European market, via Türkiye and the Black Sea. The aim is to diversify routes, triple trade flows and slash freight transit times by 2030. The Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer is a regional application of the EU Tech

The Platform brings together European technology, expertise, standards and financing to strengthen secure, trusted and resilient digital connectivity. It contributes to the EU's plans to develop the Middle Corridor, which will connect Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and directly to the European market, via Türkiye and the Black Sea. The aim is to diversify routes, triple trade flows and slash freight transit times by 2030. The Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer is a regional application of the EU Tech Business Offer as outlined in the EU International Digital Strategy , and in line with EU secure connectivity initiatives such as IRIS and policies such as the EU toolbox for 5G security. Read the full press release . Last update 11 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect
items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. items.content: Today, the European Commission hosted the second Board Meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance, following a kick-off event held in September. The Alliance is an industry-led initiative which will strengthen Europe's and Ukraine's security by accelerating the development and production of next-generation drone and counter-drone systems, and fostering partnerships in this fast-changing domain. It brings together 18 founding members, including manufacturers, innovators, start-ups and scale-ups from EU Member States, EEA EFTA countries and Ukraine, working in coordination with armed forces. During the meeting in Brussels, Andrius Kubilius , Commissioner for Defence and Space, said: “the Alliance is turning ambition into motion. Companies are signing up. By building a strong Alliance we want to forge industrial partnerships and collaboration, because Europe and Ukraine complement each other. Our strengths are greater combined than apart”. Launched during the third EU-Ukraine Defence Industry Forum in Kyiv, the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance is a first step implementing the EU-Ukraine Drone Deal announced by President Ursula von der Leyen on 15 July as part of the EU–Ukraine Defence Industrial Pact . Through it, the Commission further ensures that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs today, while strengthening Europe's defence readiness for the future. Discussions on the Alliance’s governance structure concluded successfully today with the adoption of the Terms of References and the election of the Co-chairs – Quantum Systems from the EU, and UFORCE from Ukraine . Furthermore, deep discussions were held on the Alliance’s priorities – industrial collaboration, new legal frameworks, scaling-up production to address capability needs, strengthening supply chains and cutting dependencies, joint testing and innovation, and counter-drone systems. Further information on how to join the Alliance as general members or public partners will be published shortly on the Commission's website, ahead of a third Board meeting in early 2027. Publication date 10 November 2026 Author Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space

Furthermore, deep discussions were held on the Alliance’s priorities – industrial collaboration, new legal frameworks, scaling-up production to address capability needs, strengthening supply chains and cutting dependencies, joint testing and innovation, and counter-drone systems. Further information on how to join the Alliance as general members or public partners will be published shortly on the Commission's website, ahead of a third Board meeting in early 2027. items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project.
