items.content: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 21 +15 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives. Methodology BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3). Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage. Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards. Learning from demonstrations (SFT) We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called. Learning from teachers (MOPD) Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4). Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three. Learning from rules and environments (RL stages) Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth. The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling. Data composition Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use. Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability. Results Tool use & agents BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5). Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× BFCL v4¹ 44.0 23.4 37.7 28.1 22.8 ACEBench² 58.7 30.1 55.4 39.4 24.5 τ-bench³ 51.5 23.2 46.5 6.5 28.8 Claw-Eval⁴ 46.5 39.3 48.9 31.6 31.0 BrowseComp-Plus⁵ 4.5 1.9 2.8 0.2 0.8 ToolSandbox⁶ 64.6 30.5 41.2 45.7 28.1 Average 45.0 24.7 38.8 25.3 22.7 Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined ; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Knowledge Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× GPQA Diamond⁷ 38.1 33.2 59.9 35.0 15.8 MMLU-Pro⁸ 48.9 41.6 65.5 39.4 40.0 Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Instruction following BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. Benchmark BotPsy-0.8B ours Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× IFEval⁹ 90.8 59.7 80.0 85.6 78.4 IFBench⁹ 55.9 22.0 40.9 33.9 40.6 Multi-IF¹⁰ 67.2 43.2 66.9 68.2 53.4 Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold , second best underlined . See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup. Multi-turn conversations The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1). Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5. Weak spots BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8). Where it works: app-level performance breakdown BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ. Single tool calls work well everywhere Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70). Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups. The largest gains are in multi-step tasks On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks. Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14). Inference efficiency BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer. Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each. Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier. Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9): τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer). It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks. Intended Use and Limitations BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty . BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics. items.content: Back to Articles Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models Published November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4 , my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how. This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study , which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. Table of Contents Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors Token Pooling Choosing a Pooling Budget Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Token Pooling-Aware Training A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers Optional Kernel Acceleration Using the Trained Model Evaluation Results Combining Compression Techniques References Code and Models Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document. For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together: MaxSim ⁡ ( Q , D ) = ∑ q ∈ Q max ⁡ d ∈ D q ⊤ d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim ( Q , D ) = q ∈ Q ∑ ​ d ∈ D max ​ q ⊤ d Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID , storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision. The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together. Token Pooling HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering . Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors. These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring. You can make compression proportional to document length: from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor= 4 ) With pool_factor=4 , documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged. Choosing a Pooling Budget HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls: Setting What it expresses max_tokens=16 A maximum of 16 vectors per document, including protected tokens. pool_factor=4 Approximately one quarter of each document's original vectors. distance_threshold=... A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry. This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4 , a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold , the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved. Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective . Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents : from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling model = MultiVectorEncoder( "lightonai/LateOn" ) calibration_embeddings = model.encode_document(calibration_documents) threshold = HierarchicalTokenPooling.calibrate_distance_threshold(calibration_embeddings, target_tokens= 16 ) pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(distance_threshold=threshold) # Apply pooling, targeting an average of 16 vectors per document document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents_to_index, token_pooling=pooling) Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus. Token Pooling-Aware Training Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that. If you've used Matryoshka embeddings , the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors. For my example, each training batch contributes two losses: Retrieval using the original document embeddings. Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors. I average them: L = 1 2 L u n p o o l e d + 1 2 L p o o l e d \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L = 2 1 ​ L unpooled ​ + 2 1 ​ L pooled ​ The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression. Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations. A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers: from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.losses import ( CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss, ) from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling model = MultiVectorEncoder( "answerdotai/ModernBERT-base" , similarity_fn_name= "maxsim" ) pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor= 4 ) base_loss = CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, mini_batch_size= 64 ) loss = MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss( model, base_loss, token_poolings=[ None , pooling], weights=[ 0.5 , 0.5 ], ) CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity , using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training. Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study , which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document. For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together: MaxSim ⁡ ( Q , D ) = ∑ q ∈ Q max ⁡ d ∈ D q ⊤ d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim ( Q , D ) = q ∈ Q ∑ ​ d ∈ D max ​ q ⊤ d Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID , storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors. These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring. You can make compression proportional to document length: from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor= 4 ) With pool_factor=4 , documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged. A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry. This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4 , a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold , the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective . Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. If you've used Matryoshka embeddings , the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors. For my example, each training batch contributes two losses: Retrieval using the original document embeddings. Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.14515 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models Authors: Zijian Zhang , Rizhen Hu , Jiangweizhi Peng , Shiyang Li , Sujay Bhatt , Sihan Zeng , Mingyi Hong View a PDF of the paper titled AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models, by Zijian Zhang and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold. items.content: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models Zijian Zhang Rizhen Hu Jiangweizhi Peng Shiyang Li Sujay Bhatt Sihan Zeng Mingyi Hong Affiliation: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities JPMorgan AI Research Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience: the model’s reasoning, its actions, and the feedback it receives. Both successful and failed attempts can reveal useful strategies, recurring mistakes, and inefficient behavior, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance for the model. In practice, however, their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains, rather than derived from the model’s own training experience. We introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student’s training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. The goal is to help the student learn more effectively with scaffolds during RL training, so that it performs better on its own when the scaffolds are removed at evaluation. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks. The teacher adjusts the content and amount of support as the student learns, and the resulting training experience informs the next round of diagnosis and revision. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains. Gains include 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold improves both correctness and execution efficiency, increasing the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA’s reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps, starting from the same partial solutions as QuestA but without its fixed curriculum. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class from the student’s trajectories and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold. These results suggest that a teacher can turn training experience into temporary guidance that improves the student’s independent capabilities. Preprint Figure 1: A teacher LLM helps a student LLM learn in AutoScaffold. During RL training, the frozen teacher reads the student’s training experience and writes scaffolds into its training prompts. Scaffolds are removed at evaluation. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard approach to post-training language models for reasoning and agentic tasks ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Every training step produces rich experience: the model’s reasoning, its actions, and the feedback it receives. Yet RL learns from this experience only through outcome rewards, which reduce each rollout to a single number. Much of what the rollouts reveal is lost: a failed attempt may contain useful reasoning or actions, a successful one may rely on an inefficient strategy, and on tasks that are too hard for the model, nearly every attempt fails and the reward provides no signal at all (Appendix A ). Making better use of training experience is therefore an opportunity to improve post-training beyond what rewards alone can teach. One promising way to turn such experience into guidance is training-time scaffolding , which refers to the procedure of adding auxiliary text (a scaffold ), such as a strategy, hint, or partial solution, to the prompt of the model being trained (the student ) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . A scaffold conveys what the reward alone cannot: on tasks the student cannot yet solve, it helps the student succeed so that these tasks produce learning signal, and more generally it shows the student better ways to reason and act. Scaffolds serve only to help the student learn during training and are removed at evaluation, where the student must solve tasks on its own. Figure 2: AutoScaffold: a teacher LLM designs and adapts scaffolds during RL training. (a) Unlike hand-designed scaffolding, AutoScaffold is automatic, adaptive, and unified. (b) Evaluation curves during training (success rate on ALFWorld, exact match on search-based QA), compared with GiGPO. (c) Gains over the RL baseline of each experiment, evaluated without scaffolds: success rate on ALFWorld, average exact match on search-based QA, average accuracy on math, and KernelBench correctness pass@3 averaged over Levels 1 to 3. Gray dots are prior scaffolding methods. All methods use the same student size as AutoScaffold, except Skill0, SkillRL and SkillC in ALFWorld using 7B models. (d) The teacher sets each problem’s solution-prefix ratio as instance-level scaffold: it first reveals more of the reference solutions and then withdraws support, whereas QuestA switches from 50% to 25% at a fixed step. Existing scaffolding methods, however, fall short in three respects. First, most are not automatic and do not draw on the student’s training experience: their scaffolds are prepared before training, as hand-designed hint tiers, partial solutions, or predefined skills ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . A few methods derive support from the student’s training experience, distilling trajectories into skills or generating guidance from failed attempts ( Xia et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) , but they do so through fixed pipelines. Second, they are not fully adaptive . As the student learns, its abilities change: the failures a scaffold was designed for may disappear, and new failures appear that it does not address, so a scaffold that helped early in training may no longer help the student learn. Yet support either stays fixed or changes through predefined procedures: SAGE tunes hint strength with fixed rollout-based rules ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , Skill0 withdraws skills through a predefined staged curriculum ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and SkillRL revises skills from a prescribed sample of failures without measuring their effect on the current student ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . Third, they are not unified : each is built around one task structure, such as hints or solution prefixes for mathematical reasoning or skill libraries for agentic tasks. A mathematical solution prefix, for example, does not provide the action sequencing or object-interaction strategies needed for an agentic task, so each new domain requires a new design. Deciding what support a domain needs, and how it should change over training, is therefore left to human researchers, who design scaffolds from their understanding of the domain and the model’s failures, often refining them across repeated training runs. These limitations motivate the central question of our work: How can an LLM teacher turn a student’s training experience into scaffolds, designing and adapting them throughout RL post-training, across domains, without human intervention? The difficulty is that the teacher’s ability to solve a task does not by itself tell it how to help a weaker, evolving student learn. Making scaffolding automatic , adaptive , and unified (Figure 2 a) poses three challenges. • Diagnosing the student’s bottlenecks. Aggregate rewards reveal whether the student succeeds, but not why it fails, while a few trajectories may not represent a whole task class; the teacher must decide which evidence to inspect and which failure patterns warrant intervention. • Choosing the right scaffold. The teacher must turn each diagnosis into a scaffold that suits the domain and targets either a weakness shared by a task class or a single hard task. The scaffold must also be of the right strength, because if it is too weak, every attempt may fail, and if it is too strong, every attempt may succeed. In particular, under binary outcome rewards, both cases yield identical rewards within a rollout group and no reward-based policy-gradient signal. A scaffold that is too strong can also let the student succeed without learning to solve the task on its own. • Validating and adapting scaffolds. A scaffold tailored to a few observed failures may not help the student solve other tasks in the same class, and a scaffold that helps at the current point can become unnecessary as the student improves. The teacher must assess proposed changes and decide when to revise or withdraw scaffolds, with the goal of improving the student’s performance without scaffolds. Together, these challenges make obtaining effective scaffolds non-trivial, even with access to a strong teacher. They motivate a carefully designed framework that connects diagnosis, scaffold construction, and validation throughout training, so that the scaffold remains matched to the student’s evolving needs. In this paper, we introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework in which a frozen teacher LLM observes an ongoing RL training run and automatically turns the student’s training experience into scaffolds injected into its training prompts (Figure AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models ). The approach draws on the educational principle of scaffolding: temporary, learner-contingent support that enables a learner to accomplish tasks beyond their current independent ability, and that is withdrawn as competence develops ( Wood et al., 1976 ; Vygotsky, 1978 ) . AutoScaffold automatically identifies the student’s bottlenecks and proposes new scaffolds. Every K K training steps the teacher investigates the student’s experience, using query tools to choose among training statistics, individual trajectories, groups of attempts on the same task, and its own past decisions (Figure 3 ). To choose the right scaffold, it diagnoses why the student fails and writes two levels of scaffold: class-level strategies shared across a task class, and instance-level hints for tasks the student cannot yet solve, which play complementary roles in our analysis (Appendix A ). Further, AutoScaffold also adaptively changes the content and strength of the scaffold based on the student’s current capability. The teacher revises the scaffolds every K K steps, and before deployment each class-level edit is validated on held-out tasks against no scaffold and the current scaffold, and the teacher uses these results to decide which edits to keep. It also revises how often class-level scaffolds are injected, and training with the updated scaffolds produces new experience for the next update. Finally, AutoScaffold unifies the design of the scaffold mechanism across a wide spectrum of application domains, requiring minimal domain-specific input such as the task description and the task classes at the beginning of the training. We evaluate AutoScaffold on four domains with distinct task structures and RL algorithms: ALFWorld (embodied household tasks, GiGPO), search-based question answering (GiGPO), mathematical reasoning (GRPO and DAPO), and KernelBench (GPU kernel generation, rubric-based GRPO). Under scaffold-free evaluation, AutoScaffold improves over the corresponding RL baselines in every domain (Figure 2 b,c), by 7.2 points in success rate on ALFWorld, 4.0 points in average exact match on search-based QA, up to 2.0 points in average accuracy on mathematical reasoning, and 3.0 points in correctness on KernelBench, and is competitive with or surpasses methods that rely on human-designed scaffolding. On KernelBench, it also raises the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points (Table 7 ). On mathematical reasoning, it surpasses QuestA with approximately one-third as many student training steps. Ablations show the value of interactive queries and scaffold validation, and analyses of scaffold evolution show that, given only the general principles of scaffolding, the teacher decides on its own what scaffold to give, to which tasks, and how much, and revises these decisions as the student learns (Figure 2 d). Our main contributions are as follows: • Automatic, adaptive scaffolding across domains. We introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student’s training experience into evolving scaffolds through a frozen teacher LLM. The same procedure operates across domains with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. • A design that makes the teacher’s scaffolds effective. We design a framework that consists of a number of key components, such as adaptive scaffolding based on interactive queries and decision memory, controlled injection, and held-out validation of class-level revisions. Ablation studies show that each of these components is critical for the entire system; for example, removing scaffold validation reduces ALFWorld success by 14.1 points. • Principles for effective scaffolding. Under binary rewards, we characterize conditions under which class- and instance-level scaffolds strengthen group-relative learning signals, and show how overly strong scaffolds can eliminate these signals (Appendix A ). The analysis motivates combining strategies for shared weaknesses in a task class with hints for persistently unsolved tasks, and adapting support as the student learns. • Stronger performance without scaffolds. Across embodied tasks, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold improves over the corresponding RL baselines under scaffold-free evaluation and is competitive with or surpasses scaffolding methods that rely heavily on human design, without hand-written scaffolds or hand-designed schedules. 2 Related Work AI for automating model development. LLMs increasingly improve AI systems themselves, optimizing harnesses ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , writing GPU kernels ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , and conducting parts of research ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ; Karpathy, 2026 ) . For model training, LLMs have designed rewards ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , generated environments ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and tuned hyperparameters ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , and PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) evaluates end-to-end automated post-training. Closest to our setting, LLMZero ( Fang et al., 2026 ) diagnoses training signals at each checkpoint and searches over hyperparameter transitions for GRPO, and EvoTrainer ( Chen et al., 2026b ) co-evolves the policy with a training-side harness by diagnosing rollouts and backtesting interventions. These methods operate on the training configuration or harness; AutoScaffold instead intervenes within a run at the level of task classes and instances, turning the student’s rollouts into guidance attached to its training prompts and removed at evaluation. Scaffolding in RL for LLMs. To address tasks on which nearly every rollout fails, known as the learning cliff ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , prior work supplies task-specific hints, such as tiered hints in Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , partial solutions in QuestA ( Li et al., 2026a ) and POPE ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , stepwise hints in StepHint ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and self-generated hints in SAGE ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , or reusable skills for agentic tasks ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . In most methods, the form of guidance is designed by hand for one domain, and any adaptation follows predefined rules. The closest methods are SAGE, which adjusts hint strength with rollout-based rules; SkillRL, whose teacher revises skills from a fixed sample of failures without measuring their effect; and SLIM ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , which retains, retires, or adds skills by leave-one-skill-out validation but keeps some skills at inference. In contrast, AutoScaffold lets a frozen teacher choose which evidence to inspect, applies one procedure across domains, including math and GPU kernel generation, and validates class-level proposals on the current student before deployment. Table 1 positions AutoScaffold relative to both lines of work. Table 1: Positioning of AutoScaffold. Stage : whether the method changes how a model behaves at inference time or how it is trained. What it changes : the object that is designed or edited. Granularity : whether guidance is shared by a class of tasks, specific to one task, or both. Automatic : an AI system decides the changes, without hand-designed content or schedules ( ∘ \circ : content is generated by a model, but its use follows hand-designed rules). Adapts to student progress : whether guidance or training settings are revised in response to the student’s current performance and observed failures ( ∘ \circ : changes follow predefined rules or schedules). No extra runs : changes are decided and tested within a single training run, without training separate runs or branches ( ∘ \circ : branches are trained from checkpoints). Scaffold-free eval. : the learner is evaluated without the guidance it received during training ( ∘ \circ : some guidance is kept). Domains : the task types on which the method is evaluated (A = agentic, S = search QA, M = math, K = GPU kernels). –: not applicable. Method Stage What it changes Granularity Automatic Adapts to student progress No extra runs Scaffold-free eval. QA, chem., music EvoTrainer ( Chen et al., 2026b ) training recipe, diagnostics – ✓ ✓ ✗ – M, code, SWE Scaffolding in RL for LLMs Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) training hints instance ✗ ∘ \circ ✓ ✓ M QuestA ( Li et al., 2026a ) training partial solutions instance ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ M SAGE ( Liao et al., 2026 ) training hints instance ∘ \circ ∘ \circ ✓ ✓ M SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026 ) training skills class ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ A, S Skill0 ( Lu et al., 2026 ) training skills class ✗ ∘ \circ ✓ ✓ A, S SLIM ( Shen et al., 2026 ) training skills class ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ A, S AutoScaffold (ours) training text scaffolds: skills, hints, partial solutions class + instance ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ A, S, M, K Figure 3: Overview of AutoScaffold . (a) A class-level scaffold, injected with probability q ⁡ [ C ] q[C] , and an instance-level scaffold are added to the student’s training prompt. On a hard task this turns all-failure groups into mixed groups that produce training signal; the RL algorithm is unchanged, and all scaffolds are removed at evaluation. (b) At the end of each block of K K steps, a frozen teacher gathers evidence from the training log, proposes edits, validates class-level scaffolds on held-out tasks, and deploys the updated scaffold for the next block. Bottom: an actual update on ALFWorld. 3 AutoScaffold As mentioned in the introduction, an ideal scaffolding framework should be automatic, adaptive, and unified. Each requirement places demands on AutoScaffold. Being automatic means that no human designs or reviews the scaffolds, so the teacher must find out on its own why the student fails, write the scaffolds itself, and check its own proposals before using them. Being adaptive means that the scaffold must follow the current student, so it is revised throughout training, its effect is tracked across updates, and support is withdrawn once the student no longer needs it. Being unified means that the same procedure must apply to any domain, so it relies only on minimal domain-specific information, allows different forms of textual scaffold across domains, leaves the RL algorithm unchanged, and guides the teacher with principles from our analysis rather than domain-specific rules. Figure 3 gives an overview of AutoScaffold. We describe how the student is trained with scaffolds (Section 3.1 ) and how a frozen teacher LLM designs them every K K training steps (Section 3.2 ), noting which requirement each design serves. 3.1 Scaffold-Augmented RL Training This subsection explains why scaffolds help group-relative learning and why they must adapt to the student, defines scaffolds at two levels, and describes how they are injected into training prompts. Why scaffolds help group-relative RL and why they must adapt. Group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) sample G G rollouts for a task x x and standardize each rollout’s reward by the mean and standard deviation of its group.
