items.raw_text: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models Zijian Zhang Rizhen Hu Jiangweizhi Peng Shiyang Li Sujay Bhatt Sihan Zeng Mingyi Hong Affiliation: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities JPMorgan AI Research Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience: the model’s reasoning, its actions, and the feedback it receives. Both successful and failed attempts can reveal useful strategies, recurring mistakes, and inefficient behavior, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance for the model. In practice, however, their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains, rather than derived from the model’s own training experience. We introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student’s training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. The goal is to help the student learn more effectively with scaffolds during RL training, so that it performs better on its own when the scaffolds are removed at evaluation. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks. The teacher adjusts the content and amount of support as the student learns, and the resulting training experience informs the next round of diagnosis and revision. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains. Gains include 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold improves both correctness and execution efficiency, increasing the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA’s reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps, starting from the same partial solutions as QuestA but without its fixed curriculum. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class from the student’s trajectories and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold. These results suggest that a teacher can turn training experience into temporary guidance that improves the student’s independent capabilities. Preprint Figure 1: A teacher LLM helps a student LLM learn in AutoScaffold. During RL training, the frozen teacher reads the student’s training experience and writes scaffolds into its training prompts. Scaffolds are removed at evaluation. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard approach to post-training language models for reasoning and agentic tasks ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Every training step produces rich experience: the model’s reasoning, its actions, and the feedback it receives. Yet RL learns from this experience only through outcome rewards, which reduce each rollout to a single number. Much of what the rollouts reveal is lost: a failed attempt may contain useful reasoning or actions, a successful one may rely on an inefficient strategy, and on tasks that are too hard for the model, nearly every attempt fails and the reward provides no signal at all (Appendix A ). Making better use of training experience is therefore an opportunity to improve post-training beyond what rewards alone can teach. One promising way to turn such experience into guidance is training-time scaffolding , which refers to the procedure of adding auxiliary text (a scaffold ), such as a strategy, hint, or partial solution, to the prompt of the model being trained (the student ) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . A scaffold conveys what the reward alone cannot: on tasks the student cannot yet solve, it helps the student succeed so that these tasks produce learning signal, and more generally it shows the student better ways to reason and act. Scaffolds serve only to help the student learn during training and are removed at evaluation, where the student must solve tasks on its own. Figure 2: AutoScaffold: a teacher LLM designs and adapts scaffolds during RL training. (a) Unlike hand-designed scaffolding, AutoScaffold is automatic, adaptive, and unified. (b) Evaluation curves during training (success rate on ALFWorld, exact match on search-based QA), compared with GiGPO. (c) Gains over the RL baseline of each experiment, evaluated without scaffolds: success rate on ALFWorld, average exact match on search-based QA, average accuracy on math, and KernelBench correctness pass@3 averaged over Levels 1 to 3. Gray dots are prior scaffolding methods. All methods use the same student size as AutoScaffold, except Skill0, SkillRL and SkillC in ALFWorld using 7B models. (d) The teacher sets each problem’s solution-prefix ratio as instance-level scaffold: it first reveals more of the reference solutions and then withdraws support, whereas QuestA switches from 50% to 25% at a fixed step. Existing scaffolding methods, however, fall short in three respects. First, most are not automatic and do not draw on the student’s training experience: their scaffolds are prepared before training, as hand-designed hint tiers, partial solutions, or predefined skills ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . A few methods derive support from the student’s training experience, distilling trajectories into skills or generating guidance from failed attempts ( Xia et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) , but they do so through fixed pipelines. Second, they are not fully adaptive . As the student learns, its abilities change: the failures a scaffold was designed for may disappear, and new failures appear that it does not address, so a scaffold that helped early in training may no longer help the student learn. Yet support either stays fixed or changes through predefined procedures: SAGE tunes hint strength with fixed rollout-based rules ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , Skill0 withdraws skills through a predefined staged curriculum ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , and SkillRL revises skills from a prescribed sample of failures without measuring their effect on the current student ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . Third, they are not unified : each is built around one task structure, such as hints or solution prefixes for mathematical reasoning or skill libraries for agentic tasks. A mathematical solution prefix, for example, does not provide the action sequencing or object-interaction strategies needed for an agentic task, so each new domain requires a new design. Deciding what support a domain needs, and how it should change over training, is therefore left to human researchers, who design scaffolds from their understanding of the domain and the model’s failures, often refining them across repeated training runs. These limitations motivate the central question of our work: How can an LLM teacher turn a student’s training experience into scaffolds, designing and adapting them throughout RL post-training, across domains, without human intervention? The difficulty is that the teacher’s ability to solve a task does not by itself tell it how to help a weaker, evolving student learn. Making scaffolding automatic , adaptive , and unified (Figure 2 a) poses three challenges. • Diagnosing the student’s bottlenecks. Aggregate rewards reveal whether the student succeeds, but not why it fails, while a few trajectories may not represent a whole task class; the teacher must decide which evidence to inspect and which failure patterns warrant intervention. • Choosing the right scaffold. The teacher must turn each diagnosis into a scaffold that suits the domain and targets either a weakness shared by a task class or a single hard task. The scaffold must also be of the right strength, because if it is too weak, every attempt may fail, and if it is too strong, every attempt may succeed. In particular, under binary outcome rewards, both cases yield identical rewards within a rollout group and no reward-based policy-gradient signal. A scaffold that is too strong can also let the student succeed without learning to solve the task on its own. • Validating and adapting scaffolds. A scaffold tailored to a few observed failures may not help the student solve other tasks in the same class, and a scaffold that helps at the current point can become unnecessary as the student improves. The teacher must assess proposed changes and decide when to revise or withdraw scaffolds, with the goal of improving the student’s performance without scaffolds. Together, these challenges make obtaining effective scaffolds non-trivial, even with access to a strong teacher. They motivate a carefully designed framework that connects diagnosis, scaffold construction, and validation throughout training, so that the scaffold remains matched to the student’s evolving needs. In this paper, we introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework in which a frozen teacher LLM observes an ongoing RL training run and automatically turns the student’s training experience into scaffolds injected into its training prompts (Figure AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models ). The approach draws on the educational principle of scaffolding: temporary, learner-contingent support that enables a learner to accomplish tasks beyond their current independent ability, and that is withdrawn as competence develops ( Wood et al., 1976 ; Vygotsky, 1978 ) . AutoScaffold automatically identifies the student’s bottlenecks and proposes new scaffolds. Every K K training steps the teacher investigates the student’s experience, using query tools to choose among training statistics, individual trajectories, groups of attempts on the same task, and its own past decisions (Figure 3 ). To choose the right scaffold, it diagnoses why the student fails and writes two levels of scaffold: class-level strategies shared across a task class, and instance-level hints for tasks the student cannot yet solve, which play complementary roles in our analysis (Appendix A ). Further, AutoScaffold also adaptively changes the content and strength of the scaffold based on the student’s current capability. The teacher revises the scaffolds every K K steps, and before deployment each class-level edit is validated on held-out tasks against no scaffold and the current scaffold, and the teacher uses these results to decide which edits to keep. It also revises how often class-level scaffolds are injected, and training with the updated scaffolds produces new experience for the next update. Finally, AutoScaffold unifies the design of the scaffold mechanism across a wide spectrum of application domains, requiring minimal domain-specific input such as the task description and the task classes at the beginning of the training. We evaluate AutoScaffold on four domains with distinct task structures and RL algorithms: ALFWorld (embodied household tasks, GiGPO), search-based question answering (GiGPO), mathematical reasoning (GRPO and DAPO), and KernelBench (GPU kernel generation, rubric-based GRPO). Under scaffold-free evaluation, AutoScaffold improves over the corresponding RL baselines in every domain (Figure 2 b,c), by 7.2 points in success rate on ALFWorld, 4.0 points in average exact match on search-based QA, up to 2.0 points in average accuracy on mathematical reasoning, and 3.0 points in correctness on KernelBench, and is competitive with or surpasses methods that rely on human-designed scaffolding. On KernelBench, it also raises the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points (Table 7 ). On mathematical reasoning, it surpasses QuestA with approximately one-third as many student training steps. Ablations show the value of interactive queries and scaffold validation, and analyses of scaffold evolution show that, given only the general principles of scaffolding, the teacher decides on its own what scaffold to give, to which tasks, and how much, and revises these decisions as the student learns (Figure 2 d). Our main contributions are as follows: • Automatic, adaptive scaffolding across domains. We introduce AutoScaffold , a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student’s training experience into evolving scaffolds through a frozen teacher LLM. The same procedure operates across domains with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. • A design that makes the teacher’s scaffolds effective. We design a framework that consists of a number of key components, such as adaptive scaffolding based on interactive queries and decision memory, controlled injection, and held-out validation of class-level revisions. Ablation studies show that each of these components is critical for the entire system; for example, removing scaffold validation reduces ALFWorld success by 14.1 points. • Principles for effective scaffolding. Under binary rewards, we characterize conditions under which class- and instance-level scaffolds strengthen group-relative learning signals, and show how overly strong scaffolds can eliminate these signals (Appendix A ). The analysis motivates combining strategies for shared weaknesses in a task class with hints for persistently unsolved tasks, and adapting support as the student learns. • Stronger performance without scaffolds. Across embodied tasks, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold improves over the corresponding RL baselines under scaffold-free evaluation and is competitive with or surpasses scaffolding methods that rely heavily on human design, without hand-written scaffolds or hand-designed schedules. 2 Related Work AI for automating model development. LLMs increasingly improve AI systems themselves, optimizing harnesses ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , writing GPU kernels ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , and conducting parts of research ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ; Karpathy, 2026 ) . For model training, LLMs have designed rewards ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , generated environments ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and tuned hyperparameters ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , and PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) evaluates end-to-end automated post-training. Closest to our setting, LLMZero ( Fang et al., 2026 ) diagnoses training signals at each checkpoint and searches over hyperparameter transitions for GRPO, and EvoTrainer ( Chen et al., 2026b ) co-evolves the policy with a training-side harness by diagnosing rollouts and backtesting interventions. These methods operate on the training configuration or harness; AutoScaffold instead intervenes within a run at the level of task classes and instances, turning the student’s rollouts into guidance attached to its training prompts and removed at evaluation. Scaffolding in RL for LLMs. To address tasks on which nearly every rollout fails, known as the learning cliff ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , prior work supplies task-specific hints, such as tiered hints in Scaf-GRPO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , partial solutions in QuestA ( Li et al., 2026a ) and POPE ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , stepwise hints in StepHint ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and self-generated hints in SAGE ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , or reusable skills for agentic tasks ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . In most methods, the form of guidance is designed by hand for one domain, and any adaptation follows predefined rules. The closest methods are SAGE, which adjusts hint strength with rollout-based rules; SkillRL, whose teacher revises skills from a fixed sample of failures without measuring their effect; and SLIM ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , which retains, retires, or adds skills by leave-one-skill-out validation but keeps some skills at inference. In contrast, AutoScaffold lets a frozen teacher choose which evidence to inspect, applies one procedure across domains, including math and GPU kernel generation, and validates class-level proposals on the current student before deployment. Automatic : an AI system decides the changes, without hand-designed content or schedules ( ∘ \circ : content is generated by a model, but its use follows hand-designed rules). Adapts to student progress : whether guidance or training settings are revised in response to the student’s current performance and observed failures ( ∘ \circ : changes follow predefined rules or schedules). No extra runs : changes are decided and tested within a single training run, without training separate runs or branches ( ∘ \circ : branches are trained from checkpoints). Scaffold-free eval. : the learner is evaluated without the guidance it received during training ( ∘ \circ : some guidance is kept). Lim , Allison M. Keys , Pranav Murugan , Nate Gruver View a PDF of the paper titled Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents, by Megha Srivastava and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools. Keys , Pranav Murugan , Nate Gruver View a PDF of the paper titled Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents, by Megha Srivastava and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.14508 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology Authors: Yeyuan Liu View a PDF of the paper titled When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology, by Yeyuan Liu View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there. Comments: 23 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. items.content: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure–function claims against unmeasured physiology Yeyuan Liu Affiliation: University of Virginia Email: pka5qg@virginia.edu Abstract Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner’s curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of α ′ ​ β ′ \alpha^{\prime}\beta^{\prime} cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly’s wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there. 1 Introduction A structural claim is a claim about a comparison, not only about a score. Synapse-resolution connectomes of the adult fly brain [ 1 , 2 ] have made connectome-constrained models of function practical [ 3 , 4 ] , and with them a new kind of argument. Recent studies compare models built on the measured wiring with the same models built on shuffled or rewired wiring [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . When the measured wiring performs better, the wiring is taken to matter for the function, but the conclusion depends on what the controls preserve and how the models are evaluated [ 6 ] . The comparison has a gap. A connectome fixes the graph and synapse counts. It does not fix how excitable each cell type is, how strong a synapse is per contact, how fast cells integrate, or how fast plasticity runs. These quantities can make very different circuits behave alike, and very similar circuits behave differently [ 8 , 9 ] ; connectome constraints alone underdetermine dynamics [ 10 ] . Modellers therefore choose them, usually once, and often by adjusting them until the real-connectome model performs the task. Null wirings then inherit parameters selected for the real one. Different comparisons answer different questions ( Figure 1 ). Tuning physiology until the real wiring works and transferring it to the nulls (P1) asks whether physiology tuned for one wiring fits another, and it rewards the wiring it was tuned on. Tuning each wiring on its own (P2) removes this asymmetry, but its best case may need physiology the animal does not have. Restricting the search to physiology allowed by independent data (P3) asks the biological question, provided the model still performs the task there. None of these problems can be seen at a single parameter setting, and selecting parameters on the real model’s success conditions the comparison on that success. In neuroscience this is a familiar trap in data analysis [ 11 ] , and machine learning knows it as under-tuned baselines, weight inheritance and the winner’s curse ( Section 2 ). Our aim is not to discover the bias but to measure what it does to biological conclusions drawn from connectomes, where the shared parameters are unmeasured physiology and a fair comparison must also respect what experiments constrain. Parameter choices can reverse a structural claim. In a mushroom-body model, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats cross-subtype nulls under P1 and also under P2, where each wiring is tuned on its own, the usual remedy in machine learning; it loses only under P3, and at the subtype composition implied by imaging the real-wiring model fails to learn at all. In the trained flyvis visual system, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome with a known near-real solution more than a spatially shuffled one in every one of 50 pretrained members. In a head-direction ring attractor, by contrast, the real topology is needed for a persistent bump under every protocol we test. Contributions. 1. A framework for comparing connectome-constrained models. We separate parameter transfer, independent tuning and data-constrained tuning (P1–P3, Section 3 ), state the selection and inherited-weight biases they are exposed to with closed forms for their size ( Propositions 2 and 3 ), and check these against synthetic ground truth and placebo nulls. 2. A cross-circuit test of structural claims. Across associative learning, attractor memory and motion vision, we separate conclusions that survive a change of protocol from those that reverse, and confirm the main reversal on held-out samples, model variants and spatially constrained nulls. 3. A link from protocol sensitivity to measurement and model adequacy. We identify the one unmeasured quantity that decides the fragile claim (the subtype composition of odour-responsive Kenyon cells), use published imaging to estimate it, and show that at that value the model itself fails, which no comparison between wirings can reveal on its own. Figure 1: Three protocols answer different questions, and all depend on model adequacy. Schematic for one unmeasured parameter θ \theta ; the curves are illustrative, not data. Blue: seed-averaged score of the real wiring, S ¯ R ​ ( θ ) \bar{S}_{R}(\theta) ; orange: a null, S ¯ N ​ ( θ ) \bar{S}_{N}(\theta) . P1 averages the paired difference (grey lines) over physiology selected because the real-wiring model meets the behavioural criterion, L R ​ ( θ ) ≥ c L_{R}(\theta)\geq c (blue shading), a selection that tends to favour the real wiring ( Section 4 ). P2 compares the best case of each wiring (dots; in practice the mean of the K K best parameter sets). P3 does the same within the physiology allowed by independent data, Θ data \Theta_{\mathrm{data}} (grey). Bars: physiology where the real-wiring model meets the criterion. A comparison made where it fails, as in most of Θ data \Theta_{\mathrm{data}} here, tests the model rather than the wiring. MB: mushroom-body estimates for the KC → \to MBON wiring against the identity shuffle ( Section 6.1 ). 2 Related work Connectome-constrained models of function. Lappalainen et al. [ 3 ] train ensembles of 50 visual-system models that differ in which connectivity information is given and which is learned, and evaluate them mainly by how well they predict measured neural responses. Their ensembles already address non-uniqueness of trained parameters; our question is whether that uncertainty changes verdicts about wiring. Two of their observations bear on ours: models with random network parameters but trained decoders perform consistently worse on the task, and two ensemble clusters with opposite T4c preferred directions reach nearly identical average task errors (5.297 and 5.316), so a task score alone does not identify mechanism. Whole-brain models compare the real connectome against shuffled weights that keep the global weight distribution [ 4 ] or against degree-preserving rewired graphs [ 5 ] ; an embodied brain-and-nerve-cord model keeps its published parameters for both the connectome and a degree- and sign-preserving rewiring [ 12 ] . Evolved agents have been compared against rewired graphs [ 6 ] : Park shows that what the null preserves at the sensory–motor boundary changes the verdict; there each wiring is evolved separately after matching mean activity, which corresponds to our P2, and physiology is not swept. Zhou and Hasler [ 7 ] compare representational geometry of the flyvis ensemble against weight shuffles. FlyHack [ 13 ] shows that mechanistic conclusions in flyvis depend on the trained solution and the intervention. Duan, Dong and Fiete [ 14 ] derive ring-attractor dynamics from head-direction connectivity. Yad and Nabila [ 15 ] show that differences between reconstructions of the fly compass circuit can rival differences between individuals and can break trained circuit models; this concerns uncertainty in the wiring itself, whereas we hold the wiring fixed and vary what it leaves unmeasured. None of these varies unmeasured physiology to test whether a real-versus-null verdict survives, or treats the comparison protocol as a source of bias. In macroscale network neuroscience, structure–function coupling and spatially constrained nulls are established tools [ 16 , 17 ] ; those analyses relate structural and functional maps or correlations, whereas we compare mechanistic models whose unmeasured quantities are physiological parameters. In concurrent work on human connectomes used as fixed reservoirs, Bertamini et al. [ 18 ] separate the effect of which regions are connected from that of which connection carries which weight; weight placement accounts for 28–75% of the reported adult advantage, depending on the null, while newborn connectomes keep a wiring advantage that a matched small-world graph also reaches. Their confound lies in how a null places weights, ours in how physiology is chosen for the wirings being compared; the two corrections are complementary. Closest prior work. Testing connectome structure–function claims against unmeasured physiology Yeyuan Liu Affiliation: University of Virginia Email: pka5qg@virginia.edu Abstract Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner’s curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of α ′ ​ β ′ \alpha^{\prime}\beta^{\prime} cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly’s wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there. 1 Introduction A structural claim is a claim about a comparison, not only about a score. Synapse-resolution connectomes of the adult fly brain [ 1 , 2 ] have made connectome-constrained models of function practical [ 3 , 4 ] , and with them a new kind of argument. Recent studies compare models built on the measured wiring with the same models built on shuffled or rewired wiring [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . When the measured wiring performs better, the wiring is taken to matter for the function, but the conclusion depends on what the controls preserve and how the models are evaluated [ 6 ] . The comparison has a gap. A connectome fixes the graph and synapse counts. It does not fix how excitable each cell type is, how strong a synapse is per contact, how fast cells integrate, or how fast plasticity runs. These quantities can make very different circuits behave alike, and very similar circuits behave differently [ 8 , 9 ] ; connectome constraints alone underdetermine dynamics [ 10 ] . Modellers therefore choose them, usually once, and often by adjusting them until the real-connectome model performs the task. Null wirings then inherit parameters selected for the real one. Different comparisons answer different questions ( Figure 1 ). Tuning physiology until the real wiring works and transferring it to the nulls (P1) asks whether physiology tuned for one wiring fits another, and it rewards the wiring it was tuned on. Tuning each wiring on its own (P2) removes this asymmetry, but its best case may need physiology the animal does not have. Restricting the search to physiology allowed by independent data (P3) asks the biological question, provided the model still performs the task there. None of these problems can be seen at a single parameter setting, and selecting parameters on the real model’s success conditions the comparison on that success. In neuroscience this is a familiar trap in data analysis [ 11 ] , and machine learning knows it as under-tuned baselines, weight inheritance and the winner’s curse ( Section 2 ). Our aim is not to discover the bias but to measure what it does to biological conclusions drawn from connectomes, where the shared parameters are unmeasured physiology and a fair comparison must also respect what experiments constrain. Parameter choices can reverse a structural claim. In a mushroom-body model, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats cross-subtype nulls under P1 and also under P2, where each wiring is tuned on its own, the usual remedy in machine learning; it loses only under P3, and at the subtype composition implied by imaging the real-wiring model fails to learn at all. In the trained flyvis visual system, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome with a known near-real solution more than a spatially shuffled one in every one of 50 pretrained members. In a head-direction ring attractor, by contrast, the real topology is needed for a persistent bump under every protocol we test. Contributions. 1. A framework for comparing connectome-constrained models. We separate parameter transfer, independent tuning and data-constrained tuning (P1–P3, Section 3 ), state the selection and inherited-weight biases they are exposed to with closed forms for their size ( Propositions 2 and 3 ), and check these against synthetic ground truth and placebo nulls. 2. A cross-circuit test of structural claims. Across associative learning, attractor memory and motion vision, we separate conclusions that survive a change of protocol from those that reverse, and confirm the main reversal on held-out samples, model variants and spatially constrained nulls. 3. A link from protocol sensitivity to measurement and model adequacy. We identify the one unmeasured quantity that decides the fragile claim (the subtype composition of odour-responsive Kenyon cells), use published imaging to estimate it, and show that at that value the model itself fails, which no comparison between wirings can reveal on its own. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.14514 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations Authors: Ziang Liu , James J. Kim , Yijia Dai , Jennifer J. Sun View a PDF of the paper titled Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations, by Ziang Liu and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget. Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages. Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations Ziang Liu * James J. Kim * Yijia Dai Jennifer J. Sun Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Cornell University Affiliation: codiscovery.ai/contrastive-discovery Abstract LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise , testing an empirical claim h h only against its complement ¬ h 
eg h . When evidence rejects h h , the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery , which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set , a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, 89% of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve 73% of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves 67% more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, 38 human experts chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved questions and on 82% of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. Correspondence to {zl873,jjk297}@cornell.edu . 1 Introduction Figure 1 : A contrast set turns a rejection into a resolution. A hypothesis generator proposes a contrast set of three competing explanations ( H 1 H_{1} – H 3 H_{3} ) for how X relates to Y, and coder, analyst, reviewer, and reviser agents run an experiment that produces evidence. Bars show elicited belief in each explanation before and after the same evidence. Contrastive Discovery updates belief over all three explanations and moves the lead from H 1 H_{1} (0.64) to H 2 H_{2} (0.81), so the question resolves to H 2 H_{2} and H 1 H_{1} is ruled out. Pointwise discovery updates belief only in H 1 H_{1} (0.64 to 0.07), so it records a rejection but leaves the question unresolved. See § 3 and § 4 for details. The shift toward autonomous scientific discovery has been accelerated by agents that generate hypotheses, design experiments, collect evidence, and iterate on candidate findings [ 29 , 43 , 19 , 35 ] . Recent systems scale this loop to evaluate hundreds or thousands of discoveries across scientific domains [ 2 , 11 , 17 ] . At this scale, measuring progress becomes a problem. In closed tasks, progress is measured against fixed objectives, answer keys, or benchmarks [ 33 , 45 ] , but open-ended discovery has no oracle specifying which discovery should come next. Without an oracle, progress depends not only on how each candidate is scored, but on what unit of knowledge the agent treats as learned. In most current discovery systems, that unit is a single hypothesis. The agent proposes an empirical claim h h , tests it, scores the result, and then keeps, revises, or discards h h [ 13 , 31 , 11 ] . The score may be an LLM judgment of novelty or feasibility [ 4 , 10 , 24 , 34 ] , or a belief-shift objective such as Bayesian surprise [ 2 , 18 ] , which treats discovery as evidence-induced belief change rather than a subjective judgment of interestingness. Yet the representational unit of progress stays the same: evidence updates belief in one focal hypothesis h h against its implicit complement ¬ h 
eg h . We call this pointwise discovery. This formulation is shared across agentic discovery systems that otherwise differ in how they propose hypotheses, gather evidence, and score discoveries. The pointwise representation is epistemically limiting because scientific evidence often discriminates among plausible alternatives rather than supporting a single hypothesis in isolation. This limitation is clearest when evidence rejects a proposed hypothesis h h : the agent learns that the focal hypothesis is unlikely, but not which alternative is better supported. For example, evidence against “self-employed applicants with poor credit face higher mortgage denial rates” does not say whether their denial rates are lower or no different. Under a fixed evidence-generation budget, this is information-inefficient: the agent may need additional hypothesis proposals and evaluations to resolve a scientific question that the original evidence already helps answer. We argue that open-ended discovery requires a larger unit of progress: a scientific question together with the plausible explanations that could answer it . This follows contrastive accounts of scientific explanation, in which evidence is informative because it discriminates among alternatives [ 41 , 26 ] . We introduce Contrastive Discovery , which represents each discovery step as a contrast set (Eq. 1 , Figure 1 ): a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) explanations answering one question. The agent elicits prior and posterior beliefs over the set and scores a candidate discovery by how much its evidence redistributes belief. A question is resolved when posterior belief concentrates on one explanation, so a single experiment can both rule out alternatives and identify the best-supported one. Otherwise, the evidence remains informative but the question is unresolved . Contrast sets change the unit an agent proposes and scores, not its architecture, so they can be layered onto an existing agent in two ways. As an evaluation lens , they re-evaluate evidence the agent has already collected, without modifying the agent. To guide search , they replace the agent’s hypothesis and score, so the search is rewarded for evidence that discriminates among competing explanations. We evaluate Contrastive Discovery across six domains spanning materials science, astronomy, mortgage discrimination, online discourse, software engineering practices, and social behavior. Under a shared scaffold and evidence-generation budget, pointwise baselines are guided by surprisal, novelty, or feasibility, while Contrastive Discovery is guided by belief shift over contrast sets. We find: • Pointwise rejections conceal resolvable alternatives. Across three elicitor models, a majority of pointwise proposals receive a “maybe true” prior, and 89% of the highest-surprisal pointwise candidates are rejections. Used as an evaluation lens on the same evidence, contrast sets resolve 73% of these candidates to a specific alternative without running new experiments (§ 5.1 ). • Contrastive Discovery turns rejections into resolved questions. Guiding search with contrast sets resolves 67% more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. Nearly all the gain comes from corrective resolutions, where evidence shifts support away from the explanation favored beforehand; pointwise discovery records these cases only as rejections (§ 5.2 ). • The gain comes from explicit alternatives and holds up under validation. Ablations trace the gain primarily to evaluating evidence against the full contrast set (§ 5.3 ). In a blinded study, 38 human experts chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved questions and on 82% where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped (§ 5.4 ). The gain holds when each alternative is scored independently with the pointwise scorer and at matched token and dollar cost (§ 5.5 ). 2 Open-Ended, Data-Driven Discovery Discovery loop. We study open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, where an agent uses a dataset D D to propose hypotheses h ∈ ℋ h\in\mathcal{H} , evaluates them using evidence computed from the data, and scores them, repeating under a budget of N N steps. The setting is open-ended because no predefined reward function determines the value of a discovery, which depends instead on the scientific question, the available evidence, and prior knowledge. This formulation captures recent LLM-based discovery systems [ 2 ] . Pointwise discovery. We call a discovery method pointwise when, at step t t , the agent proposes a single hypothesis h t h_{t} and independently assesses it by scoring only that proposed candidate and its evidence. Many recent LLM-based discovery approaches are pointwise , assessing each hypothesis through novelty and feasibility [ 4 , 10 , 24 ] , evidential support [ 11 , 17 ] , or Bayesian surprise [ 2 ] . In our notation (§ 3.5 ), pointwise discovery is the binary case of Contrastive Discovery, where the only alternative to h t h_{t} is its negation. The rejection case. In pointwise discovery, confirmation and rejection have different epistemic consequences. Confirmation identifies a supported explanation, but rejection only rules against the proposed one. The evidence may bear on alternatives, yet the pointwise score exposes only its effect on h t h_{t} . Resolving among competing explanations then takes a separate step for each alternative, each drawn from the finite budget of N N steps, even when one experiment’s evidence bears on all of them. 3 Contrastive Discovery We reframe a discovery step from validating a single candidate hypothesis to resolving a scientific question. We keep the evidence-induced belief-shift principle of surprisal-based discovery [ 2 , 18 ] but change the unit over which belief is represented, from one hypothesis to a structured set of plausible explanations for the same question. The alternatives thereby become part of the unit, so they determine what the evidence is compared against, how belief is updated, and what outcome the step can produce. 3.1 Constructing contrast sets At each discovery step t t , the agent poses a local scientific question and constructs a contrast set 𝒞 t = { h t , 1 , … , h t , M } , \mathcal{C}_{t}=\{h_{t,1},\ldots,h_{t,M}\}, (1) where each h t , m h_{t,m} is a plausible explanation for the same question. We require these explanations to be locally mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE): within the scope of the question, no two of them can hold at once, and together they cover the main outcomes the evidence is meant to distinguish. For example, for the scientific question “ Given a poor credit score, how is self-employment associated with mortgage denial rates? ”, the three explanations in the contrast set are that self-employed applicants face higher, no different, or lower denial rates than other applicants (further examples in Appendix ). 3.2 Eliciting beliefs over contrast sets Given a contrast set 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} , we next define the belief state used to score evidence-induced change. Before observing evidence, we elicit p t prior ∈ Δ M − 1 p_{t}^{	ext{prior}}\in\Delta^{M-1} where Δ M − 1 \Delta^{M-1} is the probability simplex over the M M explanations and p t , m prior p_{t,m}^{	ext{prior}} is the subjective belief assigned to explanation h t , m h_{t,m} . After the agent runs its experiment and observes evidence e t e_{t} , we elicit p t post ∈ Δ M − 1 p_{t}^{	ext{post}}\in\Delta^{M-1} . We treat these elicited distributions as the prior and posterior beliefs over the contrast set. Computing the posterior by Bayes’ rule would require a hand-specified likelihood model p ⁡ ( e t ∣ h t , m ) p(e_{t}\mid h_{t,m}) for every analysis. We therefore obtain each distribution directly through a constant-sum allocation task: a belief elicitor, an LLM separate from the agent (§ 4 ), assigns 100 allocation units across the explanations in 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} , first without and then with access to e t e_{t} . To reduce stochastic variance, we sample five allocations and average the normalized valid responses (see Appendices and B ). We also randomize the order of explanations during elicitation to mitigate positional bias in LLM-based evaluation (see Appendix D ). 3.3 Scoring contrastive belief shifts Because the unit of discovery is a belief distribution over competing explanations, the score should measure how evidence changes that distribution. Given prior and posterior beliefs p t prior p_{t}^{	ext{prior}} and p t post p_{t}^{	ext{post}} , we compute the Kullback–Leibler divergence ( D KL D_{\mathrm{KL}} ) of p t post p_{t}^{	ext{post}} with respect to p t prior p_{t}^{	ext{prior}} . This direction is the Bayesian surprise of Itti and Baldi [18] , the realized information gain from observing e t e_{t} . The divergence tends to grow with the size of the contrast set, reaching log 2 ⁡ M \log_{2}M bits when a uniform prior collapses onto one explanation, so we divide by log 2 ⁡ M \log_{2}M to compare sets of different sizes. We call the result the contrastive belief shift , an entropy-scaled Bayesian surprise: κ t = D KL ( p t post ∥ p t prior ) log 2 ⁡ M . \kappa_{t}= rac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{t}^{	ext{post}}\,\|\,p_{t}^{	ext{prior}})}{\log_{2}M}. We use κ t \kappa_{t} as the Contrastive Discovery score, and larger values mean that the evidence moved more belief across the competing explanations. Scaling does not bound κ t \kappa_{t} by one, because evidence can move belief onto an explanation the prior considered unlikely. When we use κ t \kappa_{t} as the tree-search reward (§ 4 ), we therefore clip it at one, r t = min ⁡ ( κ t , 1 ) r_{t}=\min(\kappa_{t},1) , and all reported information-gain analyses use the unclipped κ t \kappa_{t} (see Appendix ). 3.4 Discovery outcomes The contrastive belief shift κ t \kappa_{t} measures the magnitude of belief shift, but not the type of discovery produced by that shift. Since the prior and posterior are defined over the same competing explanations, the update can also be characterized by whether evidence confirms the prior-leading explanation, shifts support to another explanation, rules out alternatives, or leaves the question unresolved. Let m t ⋆ , prior = arg ⁡ max m ​ p t , m prior , m t ⋆ , post = arg ⁡ max m ​ p t , m post {m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{prior}}=\arg\max_{m}p_{t,m}^{\mathrm{prior}},\quad{m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{post}}=\arg\max_{m}p_{t,m}^{\mathrm{post}} denote the indices of the prior- and posterior-leading explanations. We say the question is resolved when the posterior assigns sufficient support to one explanation, max m ⁡ p t , m post ≥ τ support , \max_{m}p_{t,m}^{	ext{post}}\geq	au_{\mathrm{support}}, where τ support 	au_{\mathrm{support}} is the minimum posterior support required to identify a leading explanation (we use τ support = 0.80 	au_{\mathrm{support}}=0.80 and vary it in § 5.5 ). A resolved update is confirmative if m t ⋆ , post = m t ⋆ , prior {m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{post}}={m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{prior}} and corrective if m t ⋆ , post ≠ m t ⋆ , prior {m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{post}}
eq{m}_{t}^{\star,\mathrm{prior}} , that is, when evidence moves support from the prior-leading explanation to another one. If no explanation reaches τ support 	au_{\mathrm{support}} , the outcome is unresolved . A generated contrast set may omit the explanation the evidence supports. As a safeguard, we optionally add an abstention alternative, “none of the listed alternatives matches the evidence.” If its belief reaches τ support 	au_{\mathrm{support}} , we flag a possible omission and report no resolution. The main experiments do not include this safeguard, and § 5.4 tests it. We separately track explanations that are ruled out: an explanation h t , m h_{t,m} is ruled out when p t , m post < τ reject p_{t,m}^{	ext{post}}<	au_{\mathrm{reject}} , where τ reject 	au_{\mathrm{reject}} denotes a low posterior-support threshold (we use τ reject = 0.10 	au_{\mathrm{reject}}=0.10 ). Ruling out is tracked apart from the three outcomes above, because a single contrastive update can identify a leading explanation and also rule out competing explanations. For the pointwise setting, where a single hypothesis has scalar prior and posterior beliefs, we classify the update analogously: a hypothesis is confirmed if its posterior reaches γ support \gamma_{\mathrm{support}} , rejected if it is at most γ reject \gamma_{\mathrm{reject}} , and ambiguous otherwise (we use γ support = 0.625 \gamma_{\mathrm{support}}=0.625 and γ reject = 0.375 \gamma_{\mathrm{reject}}=0.375 , with calibration details in Appendix E ). The taxonomy thus separates how much support for a hypothesis rises or falls, which pointwise discovery captures, from which explanation the evidence favors, which requires explicit alternatives. 3.5 Pointwise discovery as the binary case Pointwise belief-shift methods score evidence by how much it changes belief in a single hypothesis h t h_{t} . In our notation, this is the binary contrast set 𝒞 t point = { h t , ¬ h t } \mathcal{C}_{t}^{\mathrm{point}}=\{h_{t},
eg h_{t}\} with belief state p t = ( p t , 1 , p t , 2 ) ∈ Δ 1 p_{t}= ig(p_{t,1},p_{t,2} ig)\in\Delta^{1} , where p t , 1 p_{t,1} is belief in h t h_{t} and p t , 2 = 1 − p t , 1 p_{t,2}=1-p_{t,1} is belief in its complement. In this representation, pointwise discovery is the M = 2 M=2 instance of Contrastive Discovery, where the only alternative ¬ h t 
eg h_{t} contains all ways the focal hypothesis could be false. Thus, when evidence weakens h t h_{t} , pointwise discovery can record negative evidence about the claim but cannot identify which alternative explanation receives that support. Contrastive Discovery replaces this complement with an explicit local partition (Eq. 1 ), so the same belief shift is distributed over named competing explanations. For pointwise belief elicitation we follow an established categorical procedure [ 2 ] : the belief elicitor rates h t h_{t} on a five-level scale (definitely false, maybe false, uncertain, maybe true, definitely true), and a “cannot comment” response counts as missing. We draw 10 10 ratings each for the prior and posterior, map them to numeric scores, fit a Beta distribution to the prior ratings, and update it with the posterior ratings. Pointwise surprisal is the normalized absolute difference in the two Beta means, and we use it as the pointwise discovery score (details in Appendix ; design comparison in Appendix O ). 4 Experimental Setup We evaluate Contrastive Discovery in an open-ended, data-driven setting: given a tabular dataset D D and metadata, we give the agent a fixed budget of N = 200 N=200 experimental validations. Each validation consists of exploring a scientific question by generating a contrast set, eliciting prior belief over the set, designing and executing an experiment to evaluate it, checking the experiment with a reviewer agent, and eliciting posterior belief. To choose which question to explore next, we use Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) [ 7 ] , following prior work on agentic scientific discovery and hypothesis search [ 2 , 43 , 10 , 39 ] and on tree search for LLM reasoning and machine learning engineering [ 14 , 20 , 40 ] . Each node is one experimental validation, and its children are follow-up contrast sets that the agent proposes from the node’s result. Search is guided by the upper-confidence bound on trees (UCT) [ 23 ] , with the clipped contrastive belief shift r t = min ⁡ ( κ t , 1 ) r_{t}=\min(\kappa_{t},1) as the node reward (reward in Appendix ; tree structure in Appendix ). Our primary evaluation metric is the number of resolved scientific questions among the K K candidates that a method’s own score ranks highest, and the resolution rate divides this number by K K . Candidates are ranked within each run, and counts are averaged over seeds within each dataset and then over the six datasets. A question is resolved when the experiment concentrates posterior belief strongly enough to identify a leading explanation ( § 3.4 ), and for pointwise baselines a confirmed hypothesis counts as resolved. Among resolved questions, we further distinguish confirmative and corrective resolutions, corresponding to belief confirmation and belief revision, respectively. Appendix F repeats the resolved-question count after semantic deduplication. Discovery agent scaffold. Our base agent is the AutoDiscovery scaffold [ 2 ] , using gpt-4o for the discovery agent backbone and a separate gpt-4o -based belief elicitor (agent details in Appendix ; prompts in Appendix P ). In Contrastive Discovery, the elicitor assigns a belief distribution over all explanations in a contrast set ( § 3.2 ); in the pointwise setting, it assigns scalar beliefs for a single hypothesis at a time to compute pointwise surprisal (see Appendix ). Baselines. We compare against pointwise baselines under the same N = 200 N=200 evidence-generation budget. In this setting, each experimental validation proposes a single hypothesis and guides MCTS using pointwise surprisal. With the number of experimental validations fixed, the comparison asks whether Contrastive Discovery resolves more questions per validation by discriminating among alternatives. To provide additional pointwise comparisons, we guide MCTS using LLM-judge scores for hypothesis novelty and feasibility, following prior work on generating and evaluating research ideas [ 4 , 10 , 16 , 24 ] and scientific hypotheses [ 11 , 34 , 44 ] (judge prompts in Appendix P.3 ). Datasets. We evaluate on six datasets spanning scientific and social domains: Materials Project [ 15 ] , SDSS Galaxy [ 36 ] , BLADE Mortgage [ 12 ] , BLADE Conversation [ 12 ] , DiscoveryBench Requirements Engineering [ 32 ] , and DiscoveryBench NLS Raw [ 32 ] . These datasets vary in feature spaces, sample sizes, and domain structure. Dataset statistics, preprocessing, and filtering criteria are reported in Appendix G . We report results on three independent runs for the first four datasets and one run on the two highest-cost datasets. 5 Results We evaluate whether Contrastive Discovery increases the epistemic yield of discovery under a fixed evidence-generation budget by tracking confirmed and rejected pointwise hypotheses, resolved and unresolved contrast sets, and ruled-out alternatives. We first show that pointwise rejections conceal alternatives that the same evidence can already resolve ( § 5.1 ). We then show that guiding search with contrast sets turns these rejections into resolved questions ( § 5.2 ). Finally, we validate the gain: ablations trace it to evaluating evidence against explicit alternatives ( § 5.3 ), resolutions agree with blinded experts and other independent references ( § 5.4 ), and the gain holds across scoring rules, matched token and dollar cost, and resolution thresholds ( § 5.5 ). 5.1 Pointwise rejections conceal resolvable alternatives Figure 2 : Pointwise discovery masks resolvable alternatives behind rejection. Left: pointwise proposals show prior collapse, with most mass in the “maybe true” bin under each of three belief elicitors (columns), while explanations in contrast sets span a broader range of prior beliefs. Right: among the top-50 hypotheses ranked by pointwise surprisal, 89% are rejected under pointwise evaluation, but re-evaluating them with a post-hoc Contrastive companion on the same evidence resolves 73% of all 50 to a specific alternative. On the Contrastive side, confirmed marks resolutions to the explanation pointwise confirmed, and ambiguous marks unresolved sets. Figure 2 (left) shows that pointwise hypothesis proposals concentrate heavily in the “maybe true” prior bin across three belief elicitors (at least 59% for each). In pointwise discovery, confirmation and rejection have different epistemic consequences. Confirmation identifies a supported explanation, but rejection only rules against the proposed one. We require these explanations to be locally mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE): within the scope of the question, no two of them can hold at once, and together they cover the main outcomes the evidence is meant to distinguish. For example, for the scientific question “ Given a poor credit score, how is self-employment associated with mortgage denial rates? ”, the three explanations in the contrast set are that self-employed applicants face higher, no different, or lower denial rates than other applicants (further examples in Appendix ). 3.2 Eliciting beliefs over contrast sets Given a contrast set 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} , we next define the belief state used to score evidence-induced change. To choose which question to explore next, we use Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) [ 7 ] , following prior work on agentic scientific discovery and hypothesis search [ 2 , 43 , 10 , 39 ] and on tree search for LLM reasoning and machine learning engineering [ 14 , 20 , 40 ] . Each node is one experimental validation, and its children are follow-up contrast sets that the agent proposes from the node’s result. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.14493 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents Authors: Howard Zhang , Chuck Arvin , Logan Brown , Mihir Bhatia , Neelu Choudhary , Lily Miao View a PDF of the paper titled Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents, by Howard Zhang and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation. items.content: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents Conference: KDD Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI; August 9–13, 2026; Jeju, Korea Proceedings of KDD Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI 2026 (KDD AgenticAI 2026) CCS: Computing methodologies Intelligent agents CCS: Software and its engineering Empirical software validation Howard Zhang Affiliation: Amazon , New York , NY , USA email: zhanhowa@amazon.com , Chuck Arvin Affiliation: Amazon , Washington , DC , USA email: chuarvin@amazon.com , Logan Brown Affiliation: Amazon , Austin , TX , USA email: logbrow@amazon.com , Mihir Bhatia Affiliation: Amazon , New York , NY , USA email: bhatimi@amazon.com , Neelu Choudhary Affiliation: Amazon , New York , NY , USA email: nlchoudh@amazon.com and Lily Miao Affiliation: Amazon , New York , NY , USA email: mwting@amazon.com 2026 Abstract. Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5 × 5\times more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation. Keywords: agent evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, evaluation stability, adversarial testing, agentic AI trustworthiness 1. Introduction 1.1. Customer Impact Statement Enterprise teams are deploying LLM-based analytics agents that generate SQL, invoke tools, and synthesize answers over sensitive business data. Incorrect outputs have direct operational consequences that often evade manual review. In this study, automated evaluation uncovered a systematic SQL generation bug (Section 4.3 ) that silently returned zero rows for an entire class of queries, a failure mode that persisted undetected through manual spot-checking because the generated SQL was syntactically valid. Prior work demonstrates that such silent text-to-SQL failures degrade downstream decision quality in business intelligence systems ( Park et al., 2025 ) , while undetected schema leakage vulnerabilities expose internal database structure to adversarial users ( Agrawal et al., 2024 ) . Today, most teams rely on ad-hoc spot-checking, which this study shows misses 9 out of 72 ground-truth failures (12.5%) that were syntactically valid but semantically wrong. This research provides an evaluation strategy that catches these errors automatically. 1.2. Research Gap and Contributions Agentic systems exhibit stochastic behavior ( Atil et al., 2024 ) and execute complex multi-step workflows involving tool usage, SQL generation, and human interaction ( Fourney et al., 2024 ) that resist simple correctness checks. Three evaluation paradigms have emerged (LLM-as-a-Judge, deterministic heuristics, and hybrid approaches), yet no systematic comparison exists of how they perform across stability, detection, and discovery for agentic systems. We present a three-phase comparative evaluation of three frameworks: Strands Evals (trace-based LLM judge), PromptFoo (text-only LLM judge with red-teaming), and Agenta (deterministic heuristics). We evaluate on two supply chain analytics agents and address three research questions: • RQ1 (Stability): How stable are evaluation outputs across repeated measurements? • RQ2 (Detection): Which framework most reliably detects known failure modes, and does the answer depend on the type of failure? • RQ3 (Discovery): Which framework most effectively surfaces unanticipated failures through automated test generation? Our key findings: (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines quality: trace-based evaluation catches 91% of failures at 10% FPR while text-only matches on recall but generates 5 × 5\times more false alarms; (2) 24 novel failures were discovered with zero overlap between functional and security testing; and (3) evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss, with 9 ground-truth failures across both agents initially mislabeled by the human reviewer and corrected after evaluator flagging. 2. At the middle level, text-only LLM judges (PromptFoo) see the agent’s response plus injected context strings. On re-review, the human confirmed the partition error and reclassified all 5. The agent_b accuracy case reveals a different failure mode. The agent calculated calibration metrics for inbound lead time forecasts but misinterpreted the direction of the calibration coefficient, reporting “well-calibrated” when the data showed systematic underbias. The human reviewer, unfamiliar with the specific metric interpretation, accepted the agent’s framing. The accuracy evaluation harness flagged the inconsistency between the calculated values and the agent’s interpretation, catching 4 errors the human missed. The Information Access Hierarchy A unifying theme across Phases 1 and 2 is that the information available to the evaluation harness determines both its stability and its detection capability. Three levels of information access produce three distinct profiles: At the lowest level, deterministic evaluation harnesses (Agenta) see only string representations. They achieve perfect stability (0.000 avg within-case std) at zero cost, but cannot discriminate between correct and incorrect open-ended responses, producing 100% FPR on accuracy and intent. The exception is SQL correctness, where hand-coded regex checks achieve 92.9% recall on structurally detectable errors (agent_a), but this requires significant custom development effort and fails on semantic errors (0% recall on agent_b). At the middle level, text-only LLM judges (PromptFoo) see the agent’s response plus injected context strings. They achieve excellent stability (0.025 avg within-case std) and perform well on requirements assessable from text alone: SQL correctness (89.3% recall) and intent understanding (2.9% FPR). But they cannot assess requirements that depend on the full execution context: faithfulness (52.1% FPR because tool result metadata lacks the actual data the agent references) and tool correctness (11.1% recall because the judge cannot infer what tools should have been used from text alone). At the highest level, trace-based LLM judges (Strands) see the full OpenTelemetry execution trace. The effort-to-value ratio does not justify a separate deterministic layer. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.14492 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows Authors: Kaiyuan Hou , Yang Ping Kuo , Indranil Bhattacharya , Rohith Nama , Arushi Gupta , Carlos D. Castillo , Prathap Ramachandra , Xiaofan Jiang , Francesco Carbone View a PDF of the paper titled ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows, by Kaiyuan Hou and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $\tau^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.14487 (cs) [Submitted on 10 Nov 2026] Title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game Authors: Muhan Gao , Hangxiao Zhu , Xinqi Su , Yu Zhang , Daniel Khashabi , Kuan-Hao Huang View a PDF of the paper titled Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game, by Muhan Gao and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.
