Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search , which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper’s core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model’s idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model’s generation ability. † † footnotetext: Equal advising. 1 Introduction Figure 1: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.4 play Re-Search on the same paper. Height reflects recovery of the paper’s idea. Green marks matching terms; red marks mismatches. While DeepSeek-V4-Flash ends up circling in a basin, GPT-5.4 recovers from a dip and reaches the summit. Research ideation is not a one-shot proposal but an iterative search interleaved with every stage of a project: researchers form hypotheses, test them, and refine them based on feedback. This process can be viewed as adaptive information seeking over a space of plausible yet unverified ideas ( Klahr and Dunbar, 1988 ) . However, existing benchmarks provide limited visibility into this iterative search. Ideation benchmarks evaluate one-shot proposals using LLM judges ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , overlooking how ideas evolve through feedback. End-to-end benchmarks involve iterative search but entangle it with coding, debugging, and experimentation ( Wijk et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Rank et al., 2026 ; Lupidi et al., 2026 ; Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ; Chan et al., 2025 ) , making it difficult to distinguish failures of ideation from failures of execution. In this work, we aim to isolate the information-seeking process from the rest of autoresearch. To this end, we introduce Re-Search , a two-player questioning game that makes every step of this process observable and measurable (Fig 1 ). The setting is a scientific variant of Twenty Questions ( Mosher and Hornsby, 1966 ; Siegler, 1977 ) , a classic paradigm in cognitive science for studying human reasoning and problem solving ( Coenen et al., 2019 ) . Given only the research problem of a published paper, an inquisitor model must rediscover the paper’s idea by asking up to 100 yes-or-no questions, while an answerer model reads the full paper and replies to the questions. Every 10 questions, the inquisitor model writes down its current best guess of the idea, which a panel of judges scores against the paper’s idea (§ 3 , see Fig 2 as an example). Success on Re-Search requires three capabilities. The model must (1) ask informative questions , which means both proposing good candidate questions and judging which of them to ask, (2) maintain an adequate hypothesis space that includes the correct idea, and (3) hill-climb along promising directions while abandoning dead ends. We evaluate six recent LLMs on 200 ICML 2026 papers. GPT-5.4 leads by a wide margin, followed by Gemma-4-31B and Claude Sonnet 4.5; the remaining three models score about two thirds as high as GPT-5.4. Yet the models share a common pattern: most progress happens within the first 30 questions, after which gains slow sharply for all but GPT-5.4, and a model’s score at question 30 largely predicts its final score. So why do models stall with 70 questions left, and which capabilities are missing? We first rule out a simple knowledge deficit: on papers where both a strong and a weak model can list the core idea beforehand, the strong model still finishes far ahead. The first clue comes from question quality . When a weak model can choose from candidate questions proposed by several models, it scores far above its own solo performance. The same pattern holds for the hypothesis space . We give models a survey of candidate directions that includes the paper’s core idea; without it, many models never reach the idea, but with it, they zero in on it within a few questions—and the weaker the model, the larger the gain. In both cases, models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot generate it on their own. The ideation traces show how hill-climbing fails: weaker models either over-exploit one direction or over-explore too many, stuck into an unproductive pattern early. Our contributions are: (1) Re-Search , a two-player questioning game that isolates research ideation from execution and makes every step of ideation observable and measurable; (2) the finding that ideation is decided early: most progress happens within the first 30 questions, and weaker models lock into either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many; and (3) a diagnosis that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment, pointing to external candidates as a direct lever for improving autoresearch systems. 2 Related Work AI scientists and their evaluation. LLM-based systems now attempt to automate research from idea to paper ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Schmidgall et al., 2025 ; Gottweis et al., 2026 ) . Most are evaluated end to end: benchmarks run an agent on a research project for hours and score the outcome ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Wijk et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Rank et al., 2026 ; Lupidi et al., 2026 ; Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ) , or grade intermediate steps against expert rubrics ( Starace et al., 2025 ; Kon et al., 2026 ; Bragg et al., 2026 ; Jansen et al., 2024 ) , and open-world environments let agents pursue long projects on their own ( Chung and Du, 2025 ) . Some of them ask agents to rediscover the findings of a hidden paper, from raw data ( Xu et al., 2026 ) or by running experiments ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . In all of these, the search for the idea is mixed with coding, debugging, and experiments, and can only be reconstructed from logs afterwards ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Re-Search isolates this search, so that each question and its effect on the idea can be observed directly. Research ideation. A separate line of work asks whether LLMs can propose research ideas. Si et al. (2025) find in a large human study that LLM ideas are judged more novel but slightly less feasible than those of experts, and benchmarks such as IdeaBench ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and the ideation stage of MLR-Bench ( Chen et al., 2025 ) rate generated ideas with LLM judges. Other systems refine ideas over several rounds, through literature-grounded review ( Baek et al., 2025 ) , planned retrieval of external knowledge ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , or multi-agent and quality-diversity search ( Chen and Zhang, 2026 ; Gumma et al., 2026 ) . These evaluations either treat ideation as a single step or guide the search with LLM feedback, and none of them has a correct answer to compare against. Like us, Yang et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2026) use recent papers as ground truth, testing whether LLMs can rediscover their hypotheses by retrieving inspirations and composing a hypothesis from them. The model receives its evidence up front, whereas in Re-Search it must find the evidence itself by asking. Concurrently, Wen et al. (2026) introduce Priced Guidance to quantify the cost of steering a model toward a paper’s core idea. The evaluated model proposes multiple-choice questions with reported answer probabilities. A guide with access to the target then selects an answer, priced at − log 2 ⁡ p selected -\log_{2}p_{\mathrm{selected}} bits. Because this cost is computed from verbalized probabilities, the resulting score reflects probability-reporting behavior as well as candidate generation. Their analysis also highlights the cost of acquiring useful candidate concepts, consistent with our finding that weaker models can use supplied candidates they struggle to propose independently. In our work, the focus is on how ideation unfolds through interaction and why progress stalls. Following the cognitive view of discovery as hypothesis search guided by experimental feedback ( Langley et al., 1987 ) , Re-Search tracks idea recovery through model-generated questions and paper-grounded feedback. Controlled interventions on candidate questions and hypotheses then examine how candidate availability and selection affect recovery, without requiring models to report answer probabilities. Information seeking and question asking. Twenty Questions and related games are standard tools for studying how people ask questions: children move from testing single hypotheses to asking questions that narrow the space ( Mosher and Hornsby, 1966 ; Ruggeri and Lombrozo, 2015 ; Ruggeri et al., 2016 ) , and people adapt their questions to the structure of the hypothesis space ( Nelson et al., 2014 ; Cohen and Lake, 2016 ; Coenen et al., 2019 ) . Recent work uses the same games to evaluate and improve LLMs ( Bertolazzi et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Mazzaccara et al., 2024 ) , often by choosing questions with high expected information gain or value of information ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Choudhury et al., 2026 ; Grand et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) ; MediQ ( Li et al., 2024 ) brings the same setting to clinical diagnosis. In these tasks, the target is an object, a diagnosis, or a board configuration from a small, known set of candidates. In Re-Search , the target is a research idea, and the model must generate the candidates itself. More broadly, LLMs in multi-turn and long-horizon settings tend to commit early and rarely recover from early mistakes ( Laban et al., 2026 ; Sinha et al., 2026 ) , although deep-research agents can also switch direction mid-trajectory ( Li et al., 2026b ) ; we find that in research ideation, early questions largely decide the outcome (§ 4.2 ). Human evaluation. We use human annotators to check the reliability of the LLM judges, by comparing 498 pairs of idea cards; for each pair, they choose the card closer to the hidden solution, or mark a tie. Their labels agree well, with a Fleiss’ κ \kappa of 0.83. In 91.2% of pairs, the LLM judges agree with the annotator majority on which card is closer, or that the two are tied. Most of the remaining pairs are ones that the annotators mark as a tie but the judges do not; when both sides prefer one card, they choose the same card in 97.8% of pairs. In this section, we describe what happens in a game; § 5 asks why most models plateau early, with controlled interventions on the candidate questions ( informative questions ) and the ideas it considers ( hypothesis space ); and § 6 examines how models follow promising directions and abandon dead ends ( hill-climbing ), through the shape of the trace. We begin with the model choices, then show how ideation develops over a game (§ 4.1 ) and that the early questions largely decide its outcome (§ 4.2 ). Model selection. We evaluate both open-weight and proprietary LLMs of different strengths: Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4. What explains this gap? We first rule out knowledge as the main cause (§ 5.1 ), then show that supplying external candidates, either as questions from other models (§ 5.2 ) or as a survey of the hypothesis space (§ 5.3 ), closes much of the gap. 5.1 Knowledge Explains Little of the Gap A strong model may simply have seen more scientific text, know more candidate ideas before the game, and turn this knowledge into an advantage in the game. To test this, we use a closed-book probe that isolates the effect of knowledge. We collect a subset of 100 papers, and focus on two models, a strong one (GPT-5.4) and a weak one (GPT-OSS-120B). Each model is provided with the research problem and asked to list ten candidate solutions, three times, for 30 candidates in total; two LLM annotators then judge whether the list contains the paper’s core idea. Knowledge does not explain the gap between models. On this 100 papers subset, GPT-5.4 scores 2.54 points higher than GPT-OSS-120B; on the 24 papers where both models list the core idea, it still scores 2.28 higher, and knowledge closes barely 10% of the gap. Therefore, knowing the idea is not enough. 5.2 Weak Models Can Pick Informative Questions § 5.1 suggests that the gap lies in how models ask. Most are evaluated end to end: benchmarks run an agent on a research project for hours and score the outcome ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Wijk et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Rank et al., 2026 ; Lupidi et al., 2026 ; Garikaparthi et al., 2026 ) , or grade intermediate steps against expert rubrics ( Starace et al., 2025 ; Kon et al., 2026 ; Bragg et al., 2026 ; Jansen et al., 2024 ) , and open-world environments let agents pursue long projects on their own ( Chung and Du, 2025 ) . Some of them ask agents to rediscover the findings of a hidden paper, from raw data ( Xu et al., 2026 ) or by running experiments ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . In all of these, the search for the idea is mixed with coding, debugging, and experiments, and can only be reconstructed from logs afterwards ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Re-Search isolates this search, so that each question and its effect on the idea can be observed directly. Research ideation. A separate line of work asks whether LLMs can propose research ideas. Si et al. (2025) find in a large human study that LLM ideas are judged more novel but slightly less feasible than those of experts, and benchmarks such as IdeaBench ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and the ideation stage of MLR-Bench ( Chen et al., 2025 ) rate generated ideas with LLM judges. Other systems refine ideas over several rounds, through literature-grounded review ( Baek et al., 2025 ) , planned retrieval of external knowledge ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , or multi-agent and quality-diversity search ( Chen and Zhang, 2026 ; Gumma et al., 2026 ) . These evaluations either treat ideation as a single step or guide the search with LLM feedback, and none of them has a correct answer to compare against. Like us, Yang et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2026) use recent papers as ground truth, testing whether LLMs can rediscover their hypotheses by retrieving inspirations and composing a hypothesis from them. The model receives its evidence up front, whereas in Re-Search it must find the evidence itself by asking. Concurrently, Wen et al. (2026) introduce Priced Guidance to quantify the cost of steering a model toward a paper’s core idea. The evaluated model proposes multiple-choice questions with reported answer probabilities. A guide with access to the target then selects an answer, priced at − log 2 ⁡ p selected -\log_{2}p_{\mathrm{selected}} bits. Because this cost is computed from verbalized probabilities, the resulting score reflects probability-reporting behavior as well as candidate generation. Their analysis also highlights the cost of acquiring useful candidate concepts, consistent with our finding that weaker models can use supplied candidates they struggle to propose independently. In our work, the focus is on how ideation unfolds through interaction and why progress stalls. Following the cognitive view of discovery as hypothesis search guided by experimental feedback ( Langley et al., 1987 ) , Re-Search tracks idea recovery through model-generated questions and paper-grounded feedback. Controlled interventions on candidate questions and hypotheses then examine how candidate availability and selection affect recovery, without requiring models to report answer probabilities. Information seeking and question asking. Twenty Questions and related games are standard tools for studying how people ask questions: children move from testing single hypotheses to asking questions that narrow the space ( Mosher and Hornsby, 1966 ; Ruggeri and Lombrozo, 2015 ; Ruggeri et al., 2016 ) , and people adapt their questions to the structure of the hypothesis space ( Nelson et al., 2014 ; Cohen and Lake, 2016 ; Coenen et al., 2019 ) . Recent work uses the same games to evaluate and improve LLMs ( Bertolazzi et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Mazzaccara et al., 2024 ) , often by choosing questions with high expected information gain or value of information ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Choudhury et al., 2026 ; Grand et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) ; MediQ ( Li et al., 2024 ) brings the same setting to clinical diagnosis. In these tasks, the target is an object, a diagnosis, or a board configuration from a small, known set of candidates. In Re-Search , the target is a research idea, and the model must generate the candidates itself. More broadly, LLMs in multi-turn and long-horizon settings tend to commit early and rarely recover from early mistakes ( Laban et al., 2026 ; Sinha et al., 2026 ) , although deep-research agents can also switch direction mid-trajectory ( Li et al., 2026b ) ; we find that in research ideation, early questions largely decide the outcome (§ 4.2 ). items.content: Data Center / Cloud Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Nov 11, 2026 By Mark Chmarny Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) now includes a qualified AI bill of materials (AIBOM) component built on the open source k8s-aibom project to track AI workloads running on Kubernetes. AICR generates version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes, while k8s-aibom observes supported AI workloads and emits CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM records with confidence tiers and evidence locators. Two stock recipes select k8s-aibom by default: h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo, with other GKE recipes able to opt in using the --runtime-inventory flag. The integration was validated with AICR v1.2.0 pinning k8s-aibom 1.6.2, demonstrating approximately four API-server requests per minute, 2.2 millicores average CPU usage, and a 28 to 34 MiB controller memory working set during steady-state observation. Namespace opt-in controls which namespaces emit AIBOM records, and the system automatically classifies workload categories and serving runtimes such as vLLM inference deployments with model and container image details. Next Steps Explore the NVIDIA AICR repository to access the platform runtime tooling. Explore the k8s-aibom repository to review the AI workload inventory project. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more As teams deploy and scale AI workloads using NVIDIA Dynamo , Kubeflow, or Slurm , tracking what actually runs requires visibility beyond the platform configuration captured in a recipe. Application teams define and update these workloads independently of the platform recipe, so a reproducible deployment bundle alone cannot establish which workload artifacts are running on each node. Mutable image tags like :latest add another layer of complexity. Two nodes can end up running different code under identical tags, and a node that pulls next week may retrieve an image that was not covered by an earlier security review. NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) , an open source modular component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , now includes a qualified AI bill of materials (AIBOM) component to close that gap. An open source project created by Google, k8s-aibom tracks AI workloads running on Kubernetes. Two stock recipes select k8s-aibom by default: h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo . Other GKE recipes can opt in during generation with --runtime-inventory enabled. Recipes selecting it can opt out with --runtime-inventory disabled. AICR turns known-good GPU platform configurations into version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles. Each recipe records the desired configuration for one hardware, cloud, OS, and intent combination: its components, version pins, values, constraints, deployment ordering, and validation expectations. AICR generates reproducible deployment artifacts from fixed recipe, catalog, and bundle inputs. Bundles include checksums; signing is optional through aicr bundle --attest . Qualification with k8s-aibom is a specific claim, not a rubber stamp. AICR binds the exact upstream source, chart, CRDs, and digest-pinned controller image as one tested set, verifies provenance against Google’s expected build identity, reviews rendered RBAC and security defaults, and exercises installation, upgrade, health, and uninstall on the deployment paths it tested. This blog will enable you to configure your Kubernetes runtime using AICR to provide a validated, performant configuration for your cluster. Figure 1. NVIDIA DSX brings together the technologies needed to design, build and operate AI factories Two ends of the same problem AICR and k8s-aibom look at different parts of the AI infrastructure lifecycle. AICR helps platform teams generate and validate known-good configurations for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes. It works at the runtime deployment layer: drivers, operators, kernels, Kubernetes components, deployment configuration. k8s-aibom looks higher up the stack and later in the lifecycle of the cluster. It watches Kubernetes workload and pod APIs and emits a CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM for each recognized AI workload. Coverage is bounded: Only supported workload kinds carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried. Coverage includes native Dynamo graphs, NIMService, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet, and CronJob resources. Tracked child workloads are combined into their owner’s AIBOM. AICR answers k8s-aibom answers Is the GPU infrastructure built from a known and validated configuration? What AI assets are actually running on that infrastructure? Table 1. The value at each level of the stack. One provides control and reproducibility of the configuration for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes, while the other adds workload discovery and traceability in that cluster. Concretely, AIBOM helps you: Find unregistered or shadow AI workloads in namespaces selected for reporting Identify models, inference runtimes, agents, and RAG components Track external AI APIs and vector databases Detect changes or drift in AI dependencies Support security reviews, incident response, and compliance audits Both projects arrived at this from opposite sides of the same problem, and recognized it as such . AICR records qualified deployment intent and evaluates it against a cluster at a point in time. k8s-aibom observes supported AI workloads and records what it found, including how confidently each attribute was determined. Neither view is sufficient for AI governance on its own, and the boundary between them is exactly where accountability is missing today. Using AICR with k8s-aibom These examples reflect AICR v1.2.0 and its catalog, which pins k8s-aibom 1.6.2. Use a CLI build matching this catalog to reproduce the examples. Start with a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster running Kubernetes 1.32 or later, with NVIDIA H100 GPU nodes using Container-Optimized OS and GKE-managed drivers and device plugins. The following workflow generates a recipe, renders it into a bundle, deploys it, and validates the result. Nothing is hand-assembled and nothing is tuned by hand. With the same AICR version, catalog, and generation inputs, recipe resolution produces the same configuration. The last step checks the cluster against it. That is the half AICR brings to this pairing: a validated GPU platform quickly and repeatably. k8s-aibom then keeps inventorying supported AI workloads. Generate the recipe aicr recipe \ --service gke \ --accelerator h100 \ --os cos \ --intent inference \ --output recipe.yaml The new k8s-aibom component is selected as part of the recipe, not bolted on afterward. You can query any resolved value without generating a file: aicr query \ --service gke --accelerator h100 --os cos --intent inference \ --selector components.k8s-aibom.version # 1.6.2 Bundle and deploy Create a deployment bundle with the default Helm deployer. Replace the example node selectors with labels present on your system and GPU node pools: aicr bundle \ --recipe recipe.yaml \ --system-node-selector nodeGroup=system-pool \ --accelerated-node-selector nodeGroup=gpu-worker \ --output ./bundles The bundle is one directory per component, ordered by the dependency graph, each carrying its values, checksums, and install script. AICR supports a number of deployers via --deployer flag, including helmfile , flux , and argocd . Verify the generated bundle, then install it: (cd ./bundles && aicr verify . && chmod +x deploy.sh && ./deploy.sh) Once deployed, the k8s-aibom controller runs in the k8s-aibom-system namespace. AICR uses the main chart’s CRDs rather than the companion k8s-aibom-crds chart. Helm bundles include a CRD apply step; Flux and Argo CD handle updates through their controllers. Helmfile, Terraform, and Fleet require the documented manual CRD update when the transition calls for it. Check the installed storage version: kubectl get crd aiboms.aibom.k8saibom.dev \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[?(@.storage==true)].name}' # v1beta1 Validate aicr snapshot --output snapshot.yaml aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml --snapshot snapshot.yaml \ --phase deployment --phase conformance The k8s-aibo m health check runs as part of the deployment phase. It requires the controller deployment to be available, the cluster-scoped AIBOMControllerConfig to report a current Ready=True , and both CRDs to report the storage version the pinned chart expects. A matching storage version does not prove the full CRD schema is current. During upgrades, also verify the target schema and check for Degraded=True with reason SchemaPredatesController ; see health and readiness . Opt a namespace in Inventory is opt-in per namespace. The label controls which namespaces emit AIBOM records; it does not narrow what the controller reads. Informers still cache workload and pod specs cluster-wide, including container arguments and inline environment values. No sink and no secret access are configured by default, so nothing leaves the cluster without an explicit decision. kubectl create namespace prod-jobs kubectl label namespace prod-jobs aibom.k8saibom.dev/enabled=true Run an inference workload Supported workloads carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried automatically when their namespace opts in. For a simple demonstration, here is a vLLM deployment serving Qwen. Note that it pulls vllm/vllm-openai:latest rather than a digest, which is not an uncommon pattern in some environments. The nvidia-h100-mega-80gb selector and toleration must match your GPU pool’s labels and taints: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: vllm-qwen namespace: prod-jobs spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: {app: vllm-qwen} template: metadata: labels: {app: vllm-qwen} spec: # Adjust to match your GPU node pool's taints and labels. tolerations: - key: dedicated operator: Equal value: gpu-workload effect: NoSchedule nodeSelector: cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-h100-mega-80gb containers: - name: vllm image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest args: ["--model", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", "--max-model-len", "4096", "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.30"] ports: - containerPort: 8000 resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: "1" volumeMounts: - {name: shm, mountPath: /dev/shm} volumes: - name: shm emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 2Gi} Save this manifest as vllm-qwen.yaml , then create the workload: kubectl apply -f vllm-qwen.yaml See the inventory After applying the workload, you can track the inventory: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aiboms.aibom.k8saibom.dev Example output: NAME WORKLOAD NAME CATEGORY RUNTIME READY AGE apps-deployment-vllm-qwen Deployment vllm-qwen inference vllm True 28m The controller automatically classified the workload category and serving runtime. One boundary worth knowing: The record is built from the workload spec, so an AIBOM can exist before any pod is running. AIBOM can appear and report Ready=True while the pod is still pulling its image. An AIBOM tells you what was declared and, once a Pod exists, what it resolved to. It does not prove successful scheduling or execution. Check the status conditions: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aibom apps-deployment-vllm-qwen \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {end}' # Ready=True Synced=True SinkFailed=False Stale=False Verify the AIBOM The document is stored inline on the resource when it is small enough, with a published SHA-256 over the canonical bytes: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aibom apps-deployment-vllm-qwen -o json > aibom.json jq -r '.status.bomDocument.inline.data' aibom.json | base64 -d > bom.json jq -r '.status.bomDocument.sha256' aibom.json shasum -a 256 bom.json | awk '{print $1}' Here’s where it all comes together: jq -r '.components[] | "\(.type)\t\(.name)"' bom.json The response should look something like this: application vllm container vllm/vllm-openai machine-learning-model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct A conventional SBOM tells you which image is running. An AIBOM tells you which model is serving and which runtime is serving it. Attributes carry one of four confidence tiers— declared , inferred , unresolved , or verified —along with an evidence locator, so reviewers can see how each claim was reached. Resource impact Upstream measured k8s-aibom v1.6.1 on GKE with NVIDIA Dynamo and AICR’s configuration. The test used CPU-only nodes with workload pods remaining pending, so these figures describe controller inventory overhead: Approximately four API-server requests per minute during a 15-min steady-state observation window Average controller CPU usage of 2.2 millicores Controller memory working set of 28 to 34 MiB One AIBOM regeneration when the tested workload’s image tag changed What comes next The integration deliberately stops short of a few things, each its own decision rather than an oversight. Signed runtime observations: The runtime AIBOM is written as a Kubernetes resource, but the observation itself is unsigned. Signing would make captured observations tamper-evident; it would not prove every workload declaration true or establish successful execution. The canonical bytes and published SHA-256 shown above make signing tractable. Connecting verified provenance: k8s-aibom can verify Sigstore signatures on model claims against operator-configured trust roots, enforce signer-identity constraints, check Rekor inclusion, and assign qualifying claims the verified confidence tier. AICR leaves this verification disabled by default. AICR can also produce transparency-logged bundle attestations when signing is enabled; connecting that platform provenance to runtime AI inventory remains future integration work. Intent and observed workloads: An AICR recipe describes deployment intent. A runtime AIBOM records observed workload specifications and available pod-status evidence. Correlating them requires shared artifact identities, freshness rules, and mapping between infrastructure and workload coverage. That comparison remains future integration work; an AIBOM does not establish successful execution or complete cluster conformance. AICR is available at NVIDIA/aicr . k8s-aibom is available at GoogleCloudPlatform/k8s-aibom . Both are open source. If you run GPU workloads on Kubernetes, this integration adds an inventory of recognized AI workloads and evidence showing how each attribute was determined. AICR binds the exact upstream source, chart, CRDs, and digest-pinned controller image as one tested set, verifies provenance against Google’s expected build identity, reviews rendered RBAC and security defaults, and exercises installation, upgrade, health, and uninstall on the deployment paths it tested. This blog will enable you to configure your Kubernetes runtime using AICR to provide a validated, performant configuration for your cluster. Figure 1. NVIDIA DSX brings together the technologies needed to design, build and operate AI factories Two ends of the same problem AICR and k8s-aibom look at different parts of the AI infrastructure lifecycle. AICR helps platform teams generate and validate known-good configurations for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes. It works at the runtime deployment layer: drivers, operators, kernels, Kubernetes components, deployment configuration. k8s-aibom looks higher up the stack and later in the lifecycle of the cluster. It watches Kubernetes workload and pod APIs and emits a CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM for each recognized AI workload. Coverage is bounded: Only supported workload kinds carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried. Coverage includes native Dynamo graphs, NIMService, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet, and CronJob resources. Tracked child workloads are combined into their owner’s AIBOM. AICR answers k8s-aibom answers Is the GPU infrastructure built from a known and validated configuration? What AI assets are actually running on that infrastructure? Table 1. The value at each level of the stack. One provides control and reproducibility of the configuration for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes, while the other adds workload discovery and traceability in that cluster. Concretely, AIBOM helps you: Find unregistered or shadow AI workloads in namespaces selected for reporting Identify models, inference runtimes, agents, and RAG components Track external AI APIs and vector databases Detect changes or drift in AI dependencies Support security reviews, incident response, and compliance audits Both projects arrived at this from opposite sides of the same problem, and recognized it as such . AICR records qualified deployment intent and evaluates it against a cluster at a point in time. k8s-aibom observes supported AI workloads and records what it found, including how confidently each attribute was determined. Neither view is sufficient for AI governance on its own, and the boundary between them is exactly where accountability is missing today. Using AICR with k8s-aibom These examples reflect AICR v1.2.0 and its catalog, which pins k8s-aibom 1.6.2. Use a CLI build matching this catalog to reproduce the examples. Start with a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster running Kubernetes 1.32 or later, with NVIDIA H100 GPU nodes using Container-Optimized OS and GKE-managed drivers and device plugins. The following workflow generates a recipe, renders it into a bundle, deploys it, and validates the result. Nothing is hand-assembled and nothing is tuned by hand. With the same AICR version, catalog, and generation inputs, recipe resolution produces the same configuration. The last step checks the cluster against it. That is the half AICR brings to this pairing: a validated GPU platform quickly and repeatably. k8s-aibom then keeps inventorying supported AI workloads. Generate the recipe aicr recipe \ --service gke \ --accelerator h100 \ --os cos \ --intent inference \ --output recipe.yaml The new k8s-aibom component is selected as part of the recipe, not bolted on afterward. You can query any resolved value without generating a file: aicr query \ --service gke --accelerator h100 --os cos --intent inference \ --selector components.k8s-aibom.version # 1.6.2 Bundle and deploy Create a deployment bundle with the default Helm deployer. Replace the example node selectors with labels present on your system and GPU node pools: aicr bundle \ --recipe recipe.yaml \ --system-node-selector nodeGroup=system-pool \ --accelerated-node-selector nodeGroup=gpu-worker \ --output ./bundles The bundle is one directory per component, ordered by the dependency graph, each carrying its values, checksums, and install script. AICR supports a number of deployers via --deployer flag, including helmfile , flux , and argocd . Verify the generated bundle, then install it: (cd ./bundles && aicr verify . && chmod +x deploy.sh && ./deploy.sh) Once deployed, the k8s-aibom controller runs in the k8s-aibom-system namespace. AICR uses the main chart’s CRDs rather than the companion k8s-aibom-crds chart. Helm bundles include a CRD apply step; Flux and Argo CD handle updates through their controllers. Helmfile, Terraform, and Fleet require the documented manual CRD update when the transition calls for it. Check the installed storage version: kubectl get crd aiboms.aibom.k8saibom.dev \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[?(@.storage==true)].name}' # v1beta1 Validate aicr snapshot --output snapshot.yaml aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml --snapshot snapshot.yaml \ --phase deployment --phase conformance The k8s-aibo m health check runs as part of the deployment phase. It requires the controller deployment to be available, the cluster-scoped AIBOMControllerConfig to report a current Ready=True , and both CRDs to report the storage version the pinned chart expects. A matching storage version does not prove the full CRD schema is current. During upgrades, also verify the target schema and check for Degraded=True with reason SchemaPredatesController ; see health and readiness . Opt a namespace in Inventory is opt-in per namespace. The label controls which namespaces emit AIBOM records; it does not narrow what the controller reads. Informers still cache workload and pod specs cluster-wide, including container arguments and inline environment values. No sink and no secret access are configured by default, so nothing leaves the cluster without an explicit decision. kubectl create namespace prod-jobs kubectl label namespace prod-jobs aibom.k8saibom.dev/enabled=true Run an inference workload Supported workloads carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried automatically when their namespace opts in. For a simple demonstration, here is a vLLM deployment serving Qwen. Note that it pulls vllm/vllm-openai:latest rather than a digest, which is not an uncommon pattern in some environments. The nvidia-h100-mega-80gb selector and toleration must match your GPU pool’s labels and taints: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: vllm-qwen namespace: prod-jobs spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: {app: vllm-qwen} template: metadata: labels: {app: vllm-qwen} spec: # Adjust to match your GPU node pool's taints and labels. tolerations: - key: dedicated operator: Equal value: gpu-workload effect: NoSchedule nodeSelector: cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-h100-mega-80gb containers: - name: vllm image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest args: ["--model", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", "--max-model-len", "4096", "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.30"] ports: - containerPort: 8000 resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: "1" volumeMounts: - {name: shm, mountPath: /dev/shm} volumes: - name: shm emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 2Gi} Save this manifest as vllm-qwen.yaml , then create the workload: kubectl apply -f vllm-qwen.yaml See the inventory After applying the workload, you can track the inventory: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aiboms.aibom.k8saibom.dev Example output: NAME WORKLOAD NAME CATEGORY RUNTIME READY AGE apps-deployment-vllm-qwen Deployment vllm-qwen inference vllm True 28m The controller automatically classified the workload category and serving runtime. One boundary worth knowing: The record is built from the workload spec, so an AIBOM can exist before any pod is running. AIBOM can appear and report Ready=True while the pod is still pulling its image. An AIBOM tells you what was declared and, once a Pod exists, what it resolved to. It does not prove successful scheduling or execution. Check the status conditions: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aibom apps-deployment-vllm-qwen \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {end}' # Ready=True Synced=True SinkFailed=False Stale=False Verify the AIBOM The document is stored inline on the resource when it is small enough, with a published SHA-256 over the canonical bytes: kubectl -n prod-jobs get aibom apps-deployment-vllm-qwen -o json > aibom.json jq -r '.status.bomDocument.inline.data' aibom.json | base64 -d > bom.json jq -r '.status.bomDocument.sha256' aibom.json shasum -a 256 bom.json | awk '{print $1}' Here’s where it all comes together: jq -r '.components[] | "\(.type)\t\(.name)"' bom.json The response should look something like this: application vllm container vllm/vllm-openai machine-learning-model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct A conventional SBOM tells you which image is running. An AIBOM tells you which model is serving and which runtime is serving it. Attributes carry one of four confidence tiers— declared , inferred , unresolved , or verified —along with an evidence locator, so reviewers can see how each claim was reached. Resource impact Upstream measured k8s-aibom v1.6.1 on GKE with NVIDIA Dynamo and AICR’s configuration. The test used CPU-only nodes with workload pods remaining pending, so these figures describe controller inventory overhead: Approximately four API-server requests per minute during a 15-min steady-state observation window Average controller CPU usage of 2.2 millicores Controller memory working set of 28 to 34 MiB One AIBOM regeneration when the tested workload’s image tag changed What comes next The integration deliberately stops short of a few things, each its own decision rather than an oversight. Signed runtime observations: The runtime AIBOM is written as a Kubernetes resource, but the observation itself is unsigned. Signing would make captured observations tamper-evident; it would not prove every workload declaration true or establish successful execution. The canonical bytes and published SHA-256 shown above make signing tractable. Connecting verified provenance: k8s-aibom can verify Sigstore signatures on model claims against operator-configured trust roots, enforce signer-identity constraints, check Rekor inclusion, and assign qualifying claims the verified confidence tier. AICR leaves this verification disabled by default. AICR can also produce transparency-logged bundle attestations when signing is enabled; connecting that platform provenance to runtime AI inventory remains future integration work. Intent and observed workloads: An AICR recipe describes deployment intent. A runtime AIBOM records observed workload specifications and available pod-status evidence. Correlating them requires shared artifact identities, freshness rules, and mapping between infrastructure and workload coverage. That comparison remains future integration work; an AIBOM does not establish successful execution or complete cluster conformance. AICR is available at NVIDIA/aicr . k8s-aibom is available at GoogleCloudPlatform/k8s-aibom . Both are open source. If you run GPU workloads on Kubernetes, this integration adds an inventory of recognized AI workloads and evidence showing how each attribute was determined.
